activity: rustproofing technique for Morris cars at a special plant in Cowley

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY'S EVENINGS JULY 18th 1949.
BRITAIN LEADS WORL IN MOTOR RUSTPROOFING TECHNIQUE
JS  18.7.49.
Morris cars coming off the assembly lines at Cowley, Oxfordshire,
are now receiving a 100% anti-rust treatment from a special plant
known as the "Rotodip" which, operated in conjunction with one of
the most up-to-date paint plants, forms an engineering project in
which Britain leads the whole world. Until the advent of this new
technique the procedure for finishing car bodies was to first
to thoroughly clean down the body to remove all grease, and to
finally rinse by hand or automatic spray, followed by a drying
process, after which the primer and finish coats of paints were
added by spray gun. This method, however, did never give complete
protection because many important parts of the body were never
reached.
Now the bodies go through the plant which consists of a tunnel
some 20 feet square and 300 feet long, which they enter in the
plain steel, greasy state, and emerge some 1 1/2 hours later having
been cleaned, rustproofed, and primer-painted inside and out,
entirely automatically. For their journey through the plant, the
bodies are mounted on a revolving spit with the bonnet, wings and
boot in position but spaced 1/4-inch from the body to allow free
circulation, and is then carried broadside through the length of
the plant on conveyor chains in such a way that the body revolves
on its own axis while passing through the machine. The process
is in two stages - first rustproofing by cleaning, rinsing and
proofing for which the bodies pass through six large tanks, and
secondly, primer-painting during which the body is dried in an
oven, cooled down, and painted.
This series of pictures illustrates the remarkable process which
the Morris engineers are confident will protect the bodies
against corrosion and paint flaking.

DAILY HERALD
ART LIBRARY
RETURNED UNDAMAGED

KENT GIRL TO WEAVE MATERIAL FOR PRINCESS ANNE'S COAT.     MJH/RS.

Miss Mary Keer, aged 24, a weaving instructress at the Cathedral
Weaving Centre, Canterbury, is to weave the clothe for a coat
for Princess Anne from ten pounds of fleece which has been shorn
from a pet lamb, called Linda at the Children's Aid Society's
Andrew Duncan Home, which was opened by the Queen when she was
Princess Elizabeth. Miss Keer will spin the raw wool into yarn
on a spinning-wheel and then weave it into material which will
eventually make up the little coat. The Queen has asked that the
coat should be white.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: Miss Mary Keer, aged 24 of Canterbury at work
on the Douglas Andrew "Kentish" loom, on which she will weave the
material for Princess Anne's coat. She is wearing a green cheviot
tweed costume, the material for which she also wove on this same

MONEY AT HIS FINGER-TIPS.... NEW MINTING OF GOLD
SOVEREIGNS - BUT NOT FOR ISSUE.

London, Eng:- To preserve the knowledge of gold coining,
which has been handed down from craftsmen to craftsmen,
a small coinage of 100,000 sovereigns has been struck
at the Royal Mint here. They will not be for issue.
They were struck from the dies used for the 1925 issue.
(This 1925 issue was struck to replace light-weight coins
in the stock of the Bank of England. The general issue
of gold coinage was suspended in 1917). - Therefore the
issue which has just been struck bears the head of King
George V.
Further small mintings will take place in the future, but
again, only for the purpose of preserving the gold coining
craft.

been completed, these sovereigns are poured into a bag to
be stored in the vaults.

activity: beer being poured down drains at Ansell's Brewery in Birmingham following a production strike

te.text:
HOLD UP COAT AGAINST LT BACKGROUND PLEASE -
& PIPE WITH BEER POURING FROM IT.

FIVE MILLION PINTS OF
WALLOP THROWN AWAY
A SAD sight for beer-
drinkers. That stuff
gurgling down the drain is
their favourite drink.
Exactly 250,000 pints of
it were poured away at
Ansell's Brewery in Birm-
ingham yesterday.
But worse is yet to come.
Another five million pints
will go down the brewery's
drains within the next few
days.
Which means that
wallop worth £370,000 is
being wasted.
Why? A spokesman for
the firm said: "Wastage
on this scale obviously
grieves our customers as
deeply as it does us."
But he explained that
the beer has been spoiled
because 1,300 production
and transport workers at
the brewery went on strike
claiming a cellarman shop
steward had been victim-
ised.
The spokesman added:
"We have had to write it
off because it would have
fallen below our high
standard."
Fresh ale should be
going out soon, because the
strikers decided at a mass
meeting last night that
they will return to work on
Monday.

Scenes at the English Steel Corporation, Ltd.,
Sheffield.  Taken in January 1940. See
"Illustrated" March 30, 1940 issue: Picture-
series "Steel Town".

Sheffield.

Birth of a steel armour plate.
Out of the inferno of a roaring furnace a livid
shape appears, blazing with unimaginable heat
and fire. It has already passed through secret
processing in the furnace and now will be fed
to the jaws of the huge rolling mill.

Every armour plate of one of our great battleships
began life like this.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

te.text:
A small portion of the 'Terylene' filament yarn produced
at the new I.C.I. plant at Wilton, undergoes an additional process
known as "throwing" or "uptwisting".  The yarn is subsequently
heated in an oven to stabilize the uptwist.  This photograph shows
the charging of the oven for twist-setting.  The plant covers an
area of 30 acres and the first unit, which has a capacity of
11,000,000 lb. of filament yarn and staple fibre a year, is now in
production.  The second unit, which will be completed during 1955,
will double the capacity.

activity: portrait of Fred Steel, a first furnace hand, in the light of his own fires at a steel works in Sheffield.

te.text:
Substitute
picture for
opening spread
of steel town

T
HE long, deep shop in the works, vast and dim,
where steel is made, where rows of furnaces
pour out their streams of running metal—this
is the heart of Sheffield, town of steel.
Before one of the furnaces stands a man whose name
is Steel. Fred Steel, first furnace hand, whose job is
one of the fiercest, most gruelling in the world. On the
left is his portrait taken in the light of his own fires.
He and his workmate had advanced before the opened
mouth of the furnace and with their twenty-foot irons
had just stilled the boiling steel. At furnace heart the
temperature reaches 1,670 degrees centigrade.
Fred Steel steps back, pushes his blue glasses from
eyes glazed with the heat; his open mouth sucks in
the cooler air, sweat covers his face, mats his hair.

activity: Mrs Florence Munro bringing a cup of tea to her husband P.J. Munro and H. Woodbridge as they build a 24-foot yacht in their back garden in Fulham.

te.text:
BACK-YARD BOAT-BUILDERS PLAN TO SAIL TO           D/HA
AUSTRALIA

Neighbours of Mr and Mrs P.J. Munro of Oxberry Avenue,
Fulham, can watch ship-building in progress  by looking
out of their back windows.  Mr. Munro, production
manager of cosmetics with a West End hairdresser, is
at present building a 24 ft. yacht in the back garden,
assisted by Mr. H. Woodbridge, and he and his wife hope
to sail to Australia.  Their only experience of sailing
so far has been on the Norfolk Broads, and Mr Munro has
been building his £500 boat from library books.  When
finished, the craft will be lifted into the lane at the
back, and launched at Putney, it is hoped this summer.

PHOTO SHOWS:  Mrs Florence Munro brings a cup of tea
for her husband, busy on his yacht-building in the back
garden. At left is Mr. H. Woodbridge, a building worker,
who is assisting him.

FOX PHOTOS    459352              16th Jan., 1952

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
REC. 17 JAN 1952
PLEASE RETURN
TO

activity: wood turner Bill Evans teaching apprentice Gwyndaf Breese how to make wooden spoons at the Welsh Folk Museum

te.text:
GREAVES.   D.H.   26/3/54.
RURAL INDUSTRIES IN WALES.
At the Welsh Folk Museum at St.Fagans, near
Cardiff, many of the old crafts are kept
alive today, and by means of an apprenticeship
system it is hoped to preserve them forever.
Bill Evans who comes from Pembrokeshire has
been a wood turner since he left school 35
years ago. He carries on the old craft at
the museum, [struck through] making wooden bows, spoons etc,
by hand, using only the most simple tools.
OPS. He is seen here with apprentice Gwyndaf
Breese age 18 of Merionethshire. He is showing
Gwyndaf how to make wooden spoons.

FOR 35 years Bill Evans has
been a wood turner, first in
his native Pembrokeshire and
now at the Welsh Folk Museum,
St. Fagan's, near Cardiff.
Here he is, teaching 18-year-old apprentice Gwyndaf Breese,
of Merioneth, to make a wooden
spoon. He uses the simplest
tools, but each of his completed
bowls, spoons and other articles
is a work of art.

ART LIBRARY
PLEASE RETURN
TO
3 APR 1954

activity: workmates 'crown' Allan Tree with coloured printing ink to mark the end of his five-year apprenticeship

te.text:
KT/RS.

CROWNING GLORY TO FIVE YEARS APPRENTICESHIP!

The time-honoured ceremony in the printing
world to mark the end of apprenticeship was carried
out this morning at noon on 21-year-old ALLAN TREE
who completed five years as an apprentice Colour
Etcher with the Half Tone Engraving Company of
Farringdon Road. ALLAN was brought down to the street
from his workshop in a dustbin, then "crowned" with
all the various coloured inks used. Afterwards, after
a clean-up, he retired with his "tormentors" to a
nearby hostelry where things were settled amicably over
a drink. ALLAN comes from SEVENOAKS, Kent.

PHOTO SHOWS.
ALLAN'S workmates "crown" him with
coloured printing ink during his "passing-out"
ceremony this morning.

FOX PHOTOS               27th NOVEMBER 1964          1.

COPYRIGHT SUPPLIED BY
FOX PHOTOS LTD

Yeovil for industrial, marine and A.R.P.
emergency power purposes. The drill, which is
so fine as to be scarcely visible, revolves at
the enormous speed of 100,000 revolutions a
minute.

officials will travel down to Yeovil next week
to inspect the new power units.

te.text:
IT used to be such a nice, modestly pleasant road, built in the
days when the more prosperous clerks and artisans were moving
out from the city centre.
Its bow windows were the outward and visible sign that its
occupants had
socially arrived.

No-one doubts what is
Britain's most pressing social
problem. It is housing.
Today the landlords meet in Harro-
gate. They will air their grievances at
the annual meeting of the Federation
of Property Owners. ("The oldest
and largest national organisation
pledged to defend private ownership
and private enterprise" as their letter-
heading proclaims.)
Their grievances will be very much
as before—there's not enough money
coming from the tenants; there's too
much Government interference.
Not all tenants will agree. In all our
big towns thousands are being forced
by housing shortage into hideous over-
crowding at high rents.
As fast as old slums are demolished
new ones are created.
No. 39, Palmerston-road, Spark-
brook, Birmingham, is typical. It pin-
points a problem repeated in the
inner suburbs of every big city where
industry demands more workers.

By SIDNEY WILLIAMS, reporting from Birmingham

Now its older resi-
dents are thinking it's
about time they moved
from Palmerston-road.
They see that what's
happened all over
inner Birmingham has
started to happen here
—the same thing that
happened in Bays-
water, Paddington,
Notting Hill, Battersea
in London, and Moss
Side in Manchester.
People who can't get
a house or a flat to
themselves are crowd-
ing in to make what
they call a home in
the one room.
The authorities call
it "multiple occupa-

te.text:
HARVESTING GOLDEN STANDARD MAIZE - SOME 50,000 COBS OF 
 GOLDEN STANDARD MAIZE BEING HARVESTED NEAR GUILDFORD.
 These are equal to those grown abroad and are the result
 of twelve years research of Mr. A. H. Kortland, a Dutch
 botanist and Poultry Farmer who escaped to this country
 from Holland after the Nazi occupation of the Low Countries.
 At this stage of growth this maize will stand up to eight
 degrees of frost without any ill effects. Many applications
 for seeds have been received from abroad including South Africa.
 This is the first time that this maize (which is essential
 for first class poultry) has been grown successfully in
 this country.

 O.P.S. Bringing in the cob harvest.
 FOX PHOTOS, Todd, SEPT. 23. 1943.

activity: Mr Stapley (left) taking delivery of a prize-winning silver rose-bowl after it had been Hall-marked.

te.text:
HALL MARK OF EXCELLENCE.      EH/HT

The silver rose-bowl, designed and made by Mr J. E. 
Stapley, of Whitstable, Kent, won the first prize
in the Worshipful Company of Goldsmiths' competition
for a £500 piece of plate to commemorate the Festival
of Britain. Mr Stapley, who is a student at the Royal
College of Art, London, called to collect his prize-
winning piece after it had been tested by assayers at
Goldsmiths' Hall, and received the "Hall-mark" which
guarantees that the silver itself is up to the 
standard of fineness required by law.

Photograph shows :- Mr Stapley (left) taking delivery
of the rose-bowl after it had been Hall-marked. The
prizewinning rosebowl is to be shown at the exhibition
of British silverwork by modern craftsmen, which opens
at Goldsmiths' Hall on July 2nd.
FOX PHOTOS JUNE 18th 51.      449111.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RCD. 1 9 JUN 1951
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

mer frock caught in the
breeze, at London Airport yester-
day to say good-bye to the Queen

when they left by Comet on a
visit to Southern Rhodesia. The
plane refuelled at Rome last
night and landed at Beirut half
an hour ahead of schedule.

SUN
PROPERTY
7 JUN 1969

Picture: Ron Burton

AS you may be reminded while mowing
the lawn this weekend, grass grows fast.
The National Institute of Agricultural
Botany know almost exactly how fast. They
have girls in their testing fields at
Cambridge who measure various species
of grass from time to time with rulers. On
the day we photographed scientific
assistants Naomi Trapman, aged 17, and
Cheryl Noon, 22, they measured 380 blades
of grass. The Institute do a lot of other
work to help farmers with their crops. But
none is as photogenic as the girls who
watch the grass grow.

SUN
COPYRIGHT
PHOTOGRAPH
BY RON BURTON

activity: 70-year-old blacksmith Nathaniel Barber working at his forge at Milford Mill, near Salisbury.

te.text:
ESTEN   D.H.   1.2.44.
NAT'S SCORE IS 25,000 not out.
In the tiny hamlet of Milford situated on the
outskirts of Salisbury lives 70 year old Nathaniel
Barber, Blacksmith for 53 years.  Nat belongs to
a fast dying profession, for blacksmiths are now
becoming a rarity.
Motor Engineer is the new term for where Nat used
to shoe over 200 horses six times a year, now only
20 come to him to be reshod.
Nat's father was a blacksmith as were four of his
eight brothers of whom he is the only one left.
In spite of the lack of horses to shoe, Nat
persuaded his 40 year old son to learn the craft
and now when Nat passes on, Ronald will become the
fourth generation of Barber - Blacksmith.
Nat boasts of the time he shoed famous racehorses
in the district.
Nat estimates that he has made and forged 25,000
shoes in his 53 years and hopes to make a few more
thousand yet.  He works from dawn till dusk six
days a week throughout the year.
There is another son, Horace, profession motor
engineer.
O.P.S.1  70 year old Nat. Barber at the forge
        at Milford Mill.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY'S EVENINGS, June 25th,

PROGRESS ON BRITAIN'S AERIAL GIANT

At the Bristol Aeroplane Works at FILTON, progress is being
made on the huge 125-ton "Brabazon I" landplane - the largest
ever to be built in Britain - which when completed will carry
100 people direct from London to New York. A special runway,
for which a complete village had to be demolished and which
will cost £2,000,000, and an assembly hall, are being con-
structed to get this giant into the air. She will have a wing-
span of 230ft (30ft longer than between the main structures
of Tower Bridge), and will be powered by eight Centaurus gas-
turbines of 2500 h.p. each. The picture shows

A view of the spacious interior of the "Brabazon" looking
toward the tail.

te.text:
ROPER                                  16.5.39

50 to 100,000 FULLY BOUND BOOKS PER WEEK.
Some of the largest Perfector printing
machines in Europe: Printing 64 pages on
each side of the sheet.
The copy from the author goes to Linotype
machines - they have a keyboard similar to
that of a typewriter - which transforms the
printed word into metal type. The type is
made up into a page form which has a
facsimile taken off it in paper flong,
from which the metal cast is produced.
Plates are assembled in special order on the
bed of the printing machine and after the
application of ink, the printed sheet is
produced.
The printed sheet goes through nearly half-
a dozen operations such as folding, gathering,
sewing and cutting, when it is transformed
into the bound copy sold to the public.
Real leather is used for the making of cases.
Real 22 carat gold is applied to the lettering.
Someofthe
Above is one of the machines used in the
Coplax process. Its object is to produce
the concave front, and the convex back and
hinge.
OPS.

te.text:
"SQUATTERS" TAKE OVER AT REGENT'S PARK
---------------------------------------
22-8-46

"SQUATTERS" have moved into an Anti-Aircraft gun
site at Primrose Hill, near Regent's Park, London.
These huts were originally intended for Polish
soldiers and their wives, but the inevitable
squatters have now taken over. They are homeless people
who take the possession of empty army huts, gun sites
etc. without waiting for any official decision about
the future of the disused military camps. The movement
has spread recently all over Britain, and a deputation
of squatters went to Whitehall to ask the Government to
clarify their legal position.

I.N.P. PHOTO SHOWS:        Mr. and Mrs. C. CLARKE and
                           family, and Mr. and Mrs. J.
                           ROCHE, who were living in a
condemned house at Chalk Farm, now have neighbouring huts,
but for the present they are feeding communally until they
are really settled in.
PICTURE BY F. MOTT.

te.text:
JAGUAR LEADS THE WORLD WITH THE NEW E-TYPE: PRODUCTION STEPPED
UP BY 50%
Presenting the new E-type Jaguar - the car that's put
Britain ahead on the road, rocketed her dollar earning exports,
and is fast becoming the latest status symbol for up-and-comers
with an eye for a jazzy means of transport.
The brain behind the E-type is Mr. William Heynes, chief
engineer who joined Jaguar boss Sir William Lyons' Coventry
team in 1935. His new design is revolutionary - built up largely
from the racing Jag - but Mr. Heynes has, with some conservatism
and some criticism, retained the old Jaguar gear box.
A rush of orders was expected, but Sir William didn't
bargain for the need to step up production by 50%. Down in the
Coventry works extra night shifts are being put on to cope with
demand.
And even though buyers in this country will probably
have to wait about a year for a new model, orders still pour in
from discerning motorists for this super sports car that looks
good, moves fast - top speed is 150mph - and only costs just
over £2000.

activity: A view of a 12,000 ton forging press for aluminium alloy with a 550 h.p. treble-ram pump in the foreground.

te.text:
XML)   INAUGURATION OF EUROPE'S LARGEST FORGING
        PRESS FOR ALUMINIUM ALLOY

Europe's newest and largest forging press for aluminium
alloy was inaugurated yesterday at the Redditch (near
Birmingham) works of High	Duty Alloys, Ltd., by
the Chairman, Sir Frank Spriggs.  Known as "Goliath,"
this 12,000-ton press, the first of its type in Great
Britain, has been designed to give working pressures of
4,000, 8,000 and 12,000 tons.  The press itself weighs
800 tons and has an overall height of 56ft. 4in.  Of
this, 42ft 9in. is above ground level and the remainder
with the hydraulic system for operating the movable
table, is concealed below ground level.  It cost more
then £500,000.

Photo shows:--   A view of the 12,000 ton press with
one of the 550 h.p. treble-ram pumps in the foreground.

activity: A wine and apple tasting event organized by the Food and Wine Society and the Farm Produce Council.

te.text:
PROPERTY OF
SUN
27 SEP 1967
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

THE FOOD and Wine
Society, together with
the Farm Produce
Council, organised a
taste-in yesterday. Wine
and apples.
There were seven wines
and nine varieties of
apples. Combinations of
each amounted to 63
separate tastings. No one,
however, appeared to take
the risk.
There was more than an
outside chance of getting
stomach ache and failing a
breathalyser test, all at
the same time.
Piled up
The apples were brought
up from Tunbridge Wells
by Mr. Ben Tompsett,
chairman of the National
Farmers' Union Kent Fruit
Committee, and piled on
dishes next to chateau-
bottled Sauternes.
There were Laxtons and
Cox's and Lord Lam-
bourns, Russets and Alling-
ton Pippins.
Among the wines to be
tried with them were a
1940 Chateau Latour
Blanc, 1939 Chateau de
Rayne and a 1949 Chateau
Rabaud.
Not all of them mixed.
Several members of the
society suffered acute
withdrawal symptoms
after the third or fourth
slice of apple.
Others, however, were
more enthusiastic. The
idea, said Mr. Claude
Morny, secretary of the
Wine and Food Society,
was to remind members of
the different varieties, and
the subtleties of taste, of
English apples.
"But I'm not suggesting
that anyone should choose
a wine merely to suit a
particular desert apple," he
added.
Afterwards Mr. Tompsett
enthused: "I have been
staggered by the know-
ledge about apples which
has been displayed here to-
night. Unfortunately, I
had little chance to taste
the wine."

activity: Ronald and Pauline Potter look out of their bedroom window.

te.text:
Family in cellar get
a house
at last
By Betty Crisp
I WENT underground at Torquay yesterday to the two rooms and a cupboard where a family of six has lived for five years "under the pavements."
The Torquay cave dwellers were happy.
They had just heard that they would get the first council house available, instead of waiting till November as the Housing ommitCtee proposed.
Mother-Mrs. Doris Potter, aged 40-telephoned eldest daughter, Jean, 20-year-old shop assistant, with the good news.
Then she went off to tell father-Mr. Tim Potter, aged 47-a chef at a holiday camp.
Pauline, 11, and Ron, nine, jumped with joy when they returned from school and heard they would soon have a proper place to keep their two pet hamsters. And Anne, 14, at the technical college, could hardly believe that she and Jean would soon have their own bedroom.
I saw the bedroom they have shared with their parents and the younger children at Wellesley-road, for five years.
Three beds
The 14ft. by 11ft. room was crammed with a single and two double beds, a wardrobe and two chests of drawers.
But the furniture could only be seen when the light was on, for this is the room Mr. Gibbings said only got light from "a grating in the pavement."
There is a wall up to street level a few inches in front of the only window with iron bars on top.
The rain splashes in, for both window and the door into the sitting-room have to be kept open in all weathers so that the Potters can breathe.
The Council was told: "It is hardly fitting that the Queen of the English Riviera (Torquay's advertising slogan) should house a family of four children in what you can practically describe as cellars."
No window
The Potters' sitting-room, 14ft. by 12ft., has a normal window opening on to the sloping ground at the back of the house. Their third "room" is a cupboard under the basement stairs, once the coal hole, where Tim Potter has fitted a gas cooker and a sink.
There is no window, or ventilation, and not enough spare space to swing a mouse.
"I can hardly believe we are going to get a council house at last," said Jean, a pretty auburn-haired girl.
"Mum and Dad were on the Torquay list years ago. Then they had to go to Birmingham to work and when they came back in May, 1950, they were told they must go on the bottom of the list again and wait five years.
"It has been so awful having no privacy, especially as we children grow older. Fancy Anne and myself with our own bedroom. A real one with a window that lets in sun and air."
DAILY HERALD July 7 1955 3
Ronald and Pauline Potter look out of their bedroom window.

te.text:
THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

ERECTING KENT'S FIRST ALUMINIUM SCHOOL
Ods 12.4.49.
The first of the five schools to be built by the Kent County Council
in aluminium prefabricated sections, is now well under way. The
school will be known as the Grays Farm County Primary School, and
is at St. Paul's Cray. The walls and roofs are of aluminium alloy
in prefabricated sections supplied by the Bristol Aeroplane (housing)
Company, and they are delivered to the site ready for erection. Thus
much time and labour, apart from materials, are saved. The block
illustrated in these pictures will house five classrooms and one
general purpose room. There will be another block housing two
classrooms and a general purpose room, an administrative wing,
assembly hall, canteen kitchen, dining hall, etc., and the whole
school will accommodate 360 children. The only brickwork will be
the external gable end walls and the boiler house, the foundations
of which can be seen in some of the pictures, which were taken
during a visit to the site today.

te.text:
CAMP PREPARED FOR ITALIAN WIVES BUT IT WAS
SEIZED BY BRITISH SQUATTERS.. 12-8-46

Thirty-six ex-Service men's families
have seized Vache Camp, Chalfont St. Giles. The
Camp was built for Americans at a cost of
£500,000, and was being prepared for the Italian
wives of [strikethrough]Italian[/strikethrough] Polish servicemen, but the British
Squatters settled in instead.

KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:- The local butcher takes
orders this morning from Mrs. P. Gray and Mrs
O. Thompson, at the camp this morning.
ML/JSS KEYSTONE
2

First tradesman to visit the ex-Servicemen's families now
settled in at Vache Camp, Chalfont St. Giles, was the butcher.
He took orders for the weekly joint from Mrs. P. Gray and
Mrs. O. Thompson.

KEYSTONE
PRESS AGENCY LTD.

activity: Vera Green, the champion shrimp peeler of Scotland, demonstrating shrimp peeling at the Hotel and Catering Exhibition at Olympia, London.

te.text:
WHAT'S her line? Those
nimble fingers hold the
clue. She is the Champion
Shrimp Peeler of Scotland.
Her output: 2,500 shrimps an
hour. Her name: Vera Green,
from Annan, Dumfries. Vera
showed how it's done yesterday
at the Hotel and Catering Ex-
hibition in London.

20.1.54.
CATERING EXHIBITION OPENS.
A CHAMPION SHRIMP PEELER.

The Hotel and Catering Exhibition opened
this morning at Olympia. Vera Green, 20, who
is Scotland's No. 1 shrimp girl, was demonstrating
her skill of shrimp peeling on the stand of W. Young
and Son. In her little home town of Annan
on the Solway Firth she is this year's champion
shrimp peeler. Competing against 40 finalists in
an annual contest at the local packing station where
she works, she won a silver cup by peeling 13 pints,
or 2,500 shrimps, in an hour.
KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:- MISS VERA GREEN, seen
piling up shrimps ready to start picking,
at Olympia today.
H Keystone. BIR/616225

KEYSTONE

activity: the pineapple plant with the careful hand of MR. WILSON in the background.

te.text:
COPYRIGHT PHOTOGRAPH
JOHN TOPHAM LTD.,
16, HATHERLEY ROAD,

SCOTTISH BANANAS ! - AND A PINEAPPLE !

BELIEVE IT OR NOT BUT BANANAS AND A PINEAPPLE ARE
BEING GROWN IN SCOTLAND - NEAR INVERNESS !
THE MAN RESPONSIBLE IS 59 YEARS OLD DAVID WILSON,
HEAD OF THE HORTICULTURAL DEPARTMENT ON THE DOCHFOUR
ESTATES NEAR INVERNESS - AND HE HAS A BANANA TREE WITH
JUST OVER 200 BANANAS IN FRUIT. IN DECEMBER LAST YEAR
HE HARVESTED A PINEAPPLE - SINCE WHEN HE HAS SUCCESSFULLY
REPLANTED THE HEAD FOR ANOTHER FRUITING PERIOD.
MR. WILSON, WHO COMMENCED HIS CAREER IN THE CLYDE
VALLEY AT THE AGE OF 14 LOOKING AFTER TOMATO PLANTS, HAS
BEEN NURSING HIS BANANA TREE SINCE 19TH JANUARY, 1965,
WHEN HE PLANTED IT IN ONE OF HIS GREENHOUSES. HE HAS
KEPT IT AT A HEAT OF NEVER LESS THAN 60 DEGREES F. AT
NIGHT AND ALMOST 80 DEGREES DURING THE DAY - WITH A
HIGH HUMIDITY. THE PINEAPPLE, WHICH HE HARVESTED ON
23RD DECEMBER LAST TOOK HIM THREE YEARS TO GROW.
HE EXPECT TH BANANAS TO BE FULLY RIPE BY THE END
OF JUNE - AND THE PINEAPPLE - ABOUT 1968.

PICTURE SHOWS:
THE PINEAPPLE PLANT - WITH THE CAREFUL HAND OF
MR. WILSON IN THE BACKGROUND.
117275   10/5/67   JOHN TOPHAM

activity: Workmen preparing blocks for the removal of a port propeller from the ship Queen Elizabeth during its annual spring clean in King George V Graving Dock.

te.text:
THE "QUEEN" GETS A SPRING CLEAN
Q. ELIZABETH IN DOCK              DG/HT

Biggest spring clean of the year has begun on the
QUEEN ELIZABETH (83,600 tons) nof off the Atlantic
and high and dry in the King George V Graving
Dock at Southampton. Every day she stays in dock,
some 1500 men are busy inside and out on the giant
Cunarder. Their jobs include : the removal and
refitting of the giant screws; scraping and
examining every one of the thousands of links in
the cables; scraping and painting the outer bottom
and sweeping six miles of carpets.

PHOTO SHOWS:- One of the port propellors suspended
after removal from the shaft. Workmen below it
are preparing the blocks for removal.
FOX PHOTOS Jan 17 1950 418762

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RCD. 1 8 JAN 1950

te.text: F192 3D Home + HOUSING. PRE WAR / Slums MISC.

A FORGOTTEN HAMLET IN THE MIDDLE OF LONDON.
TO BE DEMOLISHED.                                   21.3.35.

        Not far from the noise of the East India Dock-road is
a little piece of forgotten London; a place where trams and
buses have never been, and where motor-cars are a rarity. The
Bow Creek, it is called. It is a hamlet at the mouth of the
River Lea, with just a few hundred inhabitants. Now the L.C.C.
want to demolish it, as it is described as being one of the worst
slums in London. The houses are 120 years old.
O.P.S.    A view of the houses in Bow Creek which are
          to be demolished.        JM/S  Keystone.

activity: A Policeman on duty outside the deserted Austin works at Longbridge, Birmingham, looking up at a 'fuel thermometer' notice

te.text:
FUEL SHORTAGE CAUSES AUSTIN SHUT-DOWN : THOUSANDS OUT.

All production employees of the Austin Motor Company's works -
14,800 in all - are affected by a shut-down of the factories caused
by the coal shortage.  Stocks of fuel are said to be so low that
it will be impossible to start work again unless the present
allocation is revised and delivery increased, and the works may be
closed for several weeks.
With coal distribution crippled by blizzards, hundreds of industrial
plants throughout Britain have had to close down temporarily, and many
thousands of workers have been thrown out of work.
PHOTO SHOWS:- A Policeman on duty outside the deserted Austin works
at Longbridge, Birmingham, looking up at a "fuel thermometer" notice
which shows just how much coal they have in hand.  The indicator
now reads "Heating Reserve", which is just enough to keep the factory
from freezing-up - but allows none to work with.
CHI.                9th February, 1947.             PN-s.

COPYRIGHT
-PLANET NEWS LTD.
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON. E.C.4.

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION TUESDAY'S EVENINGS, Jan 21st.
"QUEEN ELIZABETH" OF THE AIR TAKE SHAPE
21.1.47.
In the early summer it is hoped that the Bristol "Brabazon" pro-
totype of Britain's largest airplane, will make her first flight.
Work on the giant aircraft began just over a year ago, and her
construction will have involved an outlay of £4,000,000, the
destruction of a village and a golf course, and the building of
a special runway costing £2,000,000.
She will be 177ft long with a wing span of 230ft (30ft longer than
the distance between the main structures of Tower Bridge), and
weigh 130 tons, and eight Centaurus gas-turbines of 2500 hp each
will power her. "Brabazon's" later models will carry 100 passengers
in comfort at 250 mph on Britain's Atlantic services.
In this picture what looks like the framework of a prefabricated
house is an outer wing section of the "Brabazon" in which engineers
will have access to the turbines during flight just as they do in
a surface ship. In the background nestling in a steel cradle, and
surrounded by scaffolding and platforms, is the massive fuselage.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
COPYRIGHT AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
INCORPORATING
Central News Illustrations Service,
119, FLEET STREET, LONDON, E.C.4

70 feet high, is being made for Coventry Cathedral by a team
of artists and craftsmen at the Royal College of Arts in
London. Mr Basil Spence, the architect says the designs are
"traditional yet not enormous vitality". The work is being
designed by three artists under the direction of Mr Laurence
Lee, Reader in Stained Glass at the Royal College of Arts.

Photograph shows :- Mr Keith New one of the designers seen
cutting the glass to diagram while Mr L. Lee is seen fitting
the pieces on to the screen.

ESTEN D.H.             1983-5236/73580   21.4.44.
50 M.P.H. ACROBATS THRILL LONDONERS. (Pictures
1000th part of a sec. by ordinary stage lighting).
Ernest Staig and his Flying Australian Air Aces
are at present giving Londoners a thrill with their
novel act at the Circus at the Stoll Theatre.  He
is 27 years old and is assisted by 3 others, Joe
Krzanich, Billy Sawyer and Sid Gimple.  They have
all broken bones of one sort or another in this
50 M.P.H. act. Ernest and his Brother who is a
Flying Officer in the R.A.F. first thought of the
idea in 1933, since when it has, except for a
period when Ernest was in the Army, played all
over Australia and New Zealand.  The Insurance
premium for this act is exceptionally high.
This human roundabout costs over a thousand pounds
and takes 4 hours to erect.  The great problem
at the moment is petrol, and they get an allowance
of 1/2 a pint per day.
OPS.1. Ernest Staig on motor cycle whirls his
companions round at 50 M.P.H. whilst they perform
hair raising acrobatics.

te.text:
BRITAIN is pressing on with plans that will double the
electric power carried to all parts of the country. By a
new method of transmission it should be possible, within a
few years, to meet any demand, and to bring electricity
to every home, farm and factory.
First hint of the new
development appeared in
the first report of the
British Electricity
Authority, which revealed
that experimental work
was in progress to in-
crease the voltages
carried by the transmis-
sion network.
For the past six months
Surrey people have been
puzzled by three gaunt,
bridge-like gantries in a
field near Leatherhead.
Now it can be told that these
gantries are the first signs of
the changing face of Britain—
electric-carrying bridges de-
signed to take the place of the
familiar pylons.
Gas-filled
From these 90 feet high, 120 feet
wide gantries, stationed 400 yards
apart, gas-filled cables will
carry a vastly greater voltage than
the solid cables now slung be-
tween the pylons.
The British grid today cannot
carry more than 132,000 volts.
The new method will make it
possible to transmit 275,000 volts,
more than double the present
supply.
The Surrey experiment has
proved the success of the method.
In the future similar gantries will
cross Britain to form the main
channel of electricity distribution.
First part of the national
scheme will be carried out in the
middle of England.
Work will soon start on a
stretch between West Melton,
[illegible]horne Notts, a
The new pylons for the super-grid system, erected near Leatherhead, Surrey.

HAMPTON COURT'S GREAT GRAPE            FCR/PM.
VINE WILL SHORTLY GIVE AGAIN.

On Saturday next cutting is to commence of the famous
black grapes of Hampton Court's Great Vine, and the
public will once again be able to purchase bunches of
this delicious fruit.  The Great Vine has this year
more than 600 bunches for cutting and as in previous
years the Ministry of Works will be offering bunches
of this vine's juicy black Hamburg grapes for sale to
the public.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:  Mr.TIZZARD - "Keeper of the Vine"
makes one of his final examinations of the bunches of
succulent black Hamburg grapes, in the huge glass-
house at Hampton Court. The main branch of this vine
is over 100 feet long.

te.text:
PROPERTY OF 
 DAILY HERALD 
 RECD. 10 JUN 1952 
 PLEASE RETURN 
 TO 
 ART LIBRARY

DURHAM PRODUCES DOLLAR-SAVING PIPELINE D/ TAN 
 One of the biggest contracts for large diameter steel 
 pipes ever placed in Britain has just been secured by 
 South Durham Steel and Iron Company, an old established 
 Teeside firm. The order, from the Basrah Petroleum Comp. 
 (an associate of the Iraq Petroleum Company) is for the 
 manufacture of 80 miles of 24-inch pipe weighing 17,000 
 tons, to be laid next year from the Zubair oilfield in 
 Southern Iraq to the port of Fao on the Persian Gulf, 
 near Basrah. In addition to the opening up of new and 
 increasing markets for the British steel industry, the 
 £900,000 order will mean a saving of some 2½ million dollars, 
 as hitherto most large diameter oil piping has been obtained 
 from the United States. 
 PHOTO SHOWS: A 26-foot steel plate being cold rolled to 
 form 24-inch diameter pipe at the Durham Steel and Iron Co. 
 FOX PHOTOS ART 8090 10th June, 1952

COPYRIGHT

 PHOTOS

te.text:
CHARCOAL BURNERS SERVE THE MODERN WORLD
March 21st 1956 PAR 55563-1 (Wo-R)

CHARCOAL BURNERS SERVE THE MODERN WORLD

Equipment of the kind used for centuries
is still employed by the charcoal burners
of the New Forest, Hampshire, as they
carry on their traditional trade under
the jurisdiction of the
Forestry Commission.

Though the technique of making charcoal
is old, there are new markets for
the product in modern industry.
Charcoal is used in the production
of drugs, chemicals (including nylons),
steel, fabrics and other commodities.
PICTURE SHOWS:- Charcoal burners
BERT RICHARDSON (left) and TOM WEST
emptying a kiln in King's Hat Wood, near
Beaulieu, Hampshire, as Forestry
Commission men EDWARD (left) and BOB
KITCHER, of Beaulieu, bring fresh supplies
of wood on horse-drawn carts.
Richardson and West, descended from
generations of charcoal burners, are
employed by a Reading, Berkshire, firm
of charcoal burners.
March 21st 1956 PAR 55563-1 (Wo-R)
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN EVENING
PAPERS OF THURSDAY, MARCH 22nd.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
23 MAR 1956
PLEASE RETURN

activity: the sleek nose of the Brabazon's hull in the construction shop at Filton

te.text:
126-TON 'BRABAZON' NEARS COMPLETION, WILL FLY THIS SUMMER.

Under the hands of 700 workers, the world's biggest landplane
is nearing completion at the plant of the Bristol Aeroplane
Company at Filton, Bristol.
Designed to be the aerial counterpart of the ' Queen Elizabeth' -
world's greatest ocean liner - the plane is the 'Brabazon I',
the gigantic sections of which are almost ready for final assembly.
It is expected that the 126-ton monster will take the air
for the first time in May or June and that three other
Brabazons on order will be flying on the London-New York service
of British Overseas Airways by 1950.
The Brabazon is a high-altitude, long-range low-wing cantilever
monoplane which will accommodate 70 to 100 sleeping passengers
or 120 sitting passengers in the utmost comfort.  The 143-foot
cabin will be pressurised to maintain an equivalent cabin
altitude of 8,000 feet while flying at 25,000 feet.
Crew will number 13, including five stewards.
Wingspan of the aircraft is 230 foot - almost twice that
of Britain's largest bomber, the Avro Lincoln - and the height
over the rudder is 50 foot.
Eight Bristol 'Centaurus' 18-cylinder, sleeve-valve, air-cooled
radial engines, each rated at 2,500 brake horsepower for
take-off, will give a maximum level speed of more than 300
miles an hour at 25,000 foot, an economical cruising speed
of 250 miles an hour at the same altitude, and a still-air range
of 5,000 miles.  Initial service ceiling will be 25,000 foot,
increasing as fuel is consumed.
PHOTO SHOWS:- The sleek nose of the Brabazon's hull
in the construction shop at Filton.
AND March 31st 1947 PN.r.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

COPYRIGHT
PLANET NEWS LTD.
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
FLEET ST., LONDON, E.C.4.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY'S EVENINGS, August 20th.

HARVESTING ON THE SUSSE "PRAIRIES"
20.8.47.
The present crisis has brought about the biggest Government drive
for a great increase in the production of home-grown food, and
the Prime Minister has called for a £100,000,000 step-up in this
direction by 1950-51. Since the War Office handed back, a year
ago, many acres of land which had been used for Artillery
training purposes, the East Sussex War Agricultural Committee had
been responsible for over a 1,000 acres [illegible] of corn being
grown. This is now in process of being harvested, and in this
picture, one of the biggest single "fields" in the country,
stretching for more than 200 acres across the rolling Sussex
Downs, is being harvested of its corn. The binders are starting
on the work which will be taken over by the Combine harvesters
at a later stage.

te.text:
"PASSING OUT" -AS A COOPER...ANCIENT APPRENTICE
CEREMONY IN PIMLICO..  1-9-50.

Twenty two year old RONALD BARHAM of
South Lambeth - today became a qualified cooper at
the end of his six and a half years apprenticeship.
The ancient "passing out" ceremony was carried out
at the Watney Brewery, Pimlico, in which Barham was
placed in the first barrel of his own making - and
fellow coopers enjoyed themselves by pouring various
concoctions - including oily soot over him, rolled
him around the mill room and finally his future health
and skill as a new cooper was toasted by all present..

KEY STONE PHOTO SHOWS:- RONALD BARHAM in the barrel
is well and truly annointed with the concoctions
with the aid of a mop - during the ceremony at
Pimlico today.
JSS/KEYSTONE   R/565820.

activity: stars line up to meet the Queen after a Royal Variety Show performance

te.text: After the show, the stars line up to meet the Queen. They are from right: Bob Hope, Sophie Tucker, her pianist Ted Shapiro and Edie Adams

THE world and Bernard
Delfont breathed again
yesterday. Not only was
peace saved but the Royal
Variety Show was able to
go on without the cuts
Delfont would have had to
make if the international
situation had worsened.
Bob Hope was able to include
the bit where he says: "And
then came the war," with
searchlights darting across the
stage and explosions in the
wings.
Harry Secombe, Norman
Vaughan and Terry Kendall did
their mock march as Sandhurst
cadets.
CLEAN-UP
And, above all, Edmundo Ros was
able to play the signature tune
that he has had for 22 years since
the band first started in the dark
days of 1940-the Cuban Love
Song!
Mr. Delfont who, with Leslie A.
MacDonell presented the show, was
busy during rehearsals all the
same, cleaning up a little in places.
Among those he had a quiet word
with were Mike and Bernie
Winters, Dickie Henderson,
Norman Vaughan and Sophie
Tucker.
Nothing scandalous, mind you,
a word here, a gesture there.
"Very funny, but OUT," said Mr.
Delfont.
Brimming with hokum, laced
with sentiment, the best of what's
left of variety went on at the
Palladium undimmed.
And next Sunday, the television
audience can join the Queen,
Prince Philip and those of her
subjects who were last night able
to afford anything from one to 20
guineas for a ticket.
They will see Harry Secombe,
magnificent in Canadian Mountie
uniform, sing a duet from Rose
Marie, with Eartha Kitt; they will
see Eartha Kitt draping 15ft. of
chinchilla fur around her neck to
sing I'm Just An Old-fashioned
Girl; and Bob Hope telling Edie
Adams that this week the Chang-
ing of the Guard is being done
outside the American Embassy.
INCOMPARABLE
But most of all, and best of
all, they will see the incomparable
Sophie Tucker, resplendent in
silver-blue gown with matching
mink, singing her life story.
Every word came out clear as a
cannon in that husky, red-hot-
momma voice that told the saga of
Sophie in 11 minutes of command-
ing presence, sly humour, perfect
timing, and noble womanhood—
even if she is 74.
SPECTACLES
There were other moments, too—
Dickie Henderson's fooling, Cliff
Richard, introduced by his group
The Shadows as "our vocalist," the
splendid Johnny Dankworth band
with the equally splendid Cleo
Laine—who after a false start
("just nerves") gave one of the
smoothest performances of the
evening.
And the spectacles—The Black
and White Minstrels closing the
first half in a riot of pink and
white plumes and the Edmundo
Ros orchestra and dancers opening
the second with a whirl of Latin-
American rhythm.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
29 OCT 1962
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

activity: Mrs. Caroline Vines and Mrs. Helen Holmes moving furniture into a Nissen hut on St. Paul's Road, Peterborough.

te.text:
MORE FURNITURE GOES INTO ARMY HUTS DESPITE QUIT NOTICES.

A policy of 'sit tight' and await developments has been adopted
by ex Servicemen who, with their wives and children, have moved
into unoccupied military huts in St. Paul's Road, Peterborough,
Northamptonshire, because they were unable to find other
accommodation as a result of the housing shortage. Notices to
quit have been served on some of the 'squatters', and German
prisoners have been brought in by the military authorities to
start pulling down huts on the site scheduled for demolition.
Among the families installed are Mr. and Mrs. Harry Joseph Vines
and their 3 1/2-year-old daughter Patricia. Mr. Vines, now an
inspector in a Diesel factory, is a former Petty Officer in the
Navy who won the British Empire Medal for bringing a lifeboat
safely to land after it had been 39 days in the Atlantic following
the torpedoing of a troopship. While recovering from his ordeal
in New York he met Caroline - now his wife, who comes from Brooklyn.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Mrs. Caroline Vines (second from right) assisted
by Mrs. Helen Holmes (on right), also in occupation of a hut, and
the children of other neighbours as she moves furniture into one
of the Nissen huts.

activity: A Blue coat boy feeding a sow with her litter on the school farm at Horsham.

te.text:
LIFE AT THE BLUECOAT SCHOOL.

Christ's Hospital or "Blue Coat School", was founded by
Edward VI on the site of an old Greyfriars monastery, and down
to a few years ago was one of London's best known scholastic
institutions. It was pulled down to make room for extensions
of St. Bartholomew's Hospital and the new General Post Office,
in Newgate Street. The School is now carried on at HORSHAM in
an imposing building. Besides the usual subjects included in
any school curriculum, the boys are taught interesting things,
such as clay modelling, carpentry, weaving, spinning etc., and
have taken advantage of their move into the country by acquiring
a farm, the work on which is done by the boys. The school has
a band complete with mace bearer and this is a familiar sight
once a year in London when the school marches through the City to
their annual church service. The boys still wear the picturesque
costume of knee breeches, yellow stockings and blue coats.

O.P.S.  A Blue coat boy feeding a sow with her litter
         on the school farm at HORSHAM..  YHD/B. KEYSTONE.

activity: Stage one of the housing programme for skilled workers manufacture of Armstrong Siddeley "Sapphire" engines, showing prefabricated house structures.

te.text:
HOUSING ESTATE FOR JET ENGINEERS.           EH/MEA

Not a brick kiln, but a housed estate in the making at 
Brockworth, near Gloucester. Houses are being massed produced 
to house skilled workers for the manufacture of Armstrong 
Siddeley "Sapphire" engines. Work is being carried out by 
Hawksley Constructions. While the houses appear to be traditional 
they are largely prefabricated. The inner walls partitions and 
roof are factory made and after erection of the inner shell, an 
outter shell of brick is added. Chimneys are built on the ground 
then lifted on to the roof by crane.

Photograph shows :- Stage one of the housing programme. The 
stacks stand like bricks awaiting the kiln instead of for the 
remainder of the house to be added.
FOX PHOTOS   JAN 7th 53.           476062

PROPERTY 
OF 
DAILY HERALD 
- 8 JAN 1953 
PLEASE RETURN TO 
ART LIBRARY

activity: An artist's impression of a transatlantic flying boat base and composite aircraft in flight.

te.text:
MALINDINE. 4. 12. 35.

An artist's impression of
a Flying Base in the Atlantic.

FOR TRANSATLANTIC AIR SERVICE.—Secrets of the lead which Britain is giving
to commercial air development will be revealed at to-day's exhibition of wonderful
models which Imperial Airways are holding at the Science Museum, South Kensington.
This illustration by W. E. Truby, a "Daily Herald" artist, is inspired by the ambitious
transatlantic air scheme. The composite aircraft, seen in flight over a flying boat base,
is now being built by Messrs. Short Bros., for Imperial Airways. It consists of two
machines a small, high-speed monoplane with a heavy fuel and mail load and a huge
flying boat carrying practically no load. The small plane, unable to rise alone with its
heavy load, is lifted by the mother machine to a height of 10.000 feet and then launched
on its way.

Photograph.
Number Z3892
(TO BE QUOTED WHEN ORDERING)

activity: Three girls starting work selling men's shirts to retailers, dressed as commercial travellers in bowler hats.

te.text:
News
From EURO PUBLICITY LIMITED - 283a HIGH STREET - CROYDON - SURREY
Telephones : MUNicipal 3022/3/4 Telegrams : "EURO CROYDON"

RECEIVED
30 DEC 1963
D. H. EDITORIAL DEPT.

For Immediate Release
24th December, 1963.
Length - 200 words
Girls in Bowlers Sell Shirts
Three smart girls who hope to beat the men at their own
game have started work in a new job selling men's shirts to
retailers. They are the first of a team to be taken on by
Cornes and Company, 18, Finsbury Circus, London, E.C.2.
The girls have been fitted out for their parts as
commercial travellers and their appearance in the City is
expected to cause much comment.
From the left they are, Jean Radcliffe (19) of Watford
Way, Mill Hill; Anne Marchmont (21) of Upper Richmond Road, Sheen,
and Rosemary Dewhurst (19) of Sherwood Park Road, Mitcham.
All the girls have worked in the drapery trade.
They will also meet buyers at a party where the non-
creasing character of the product will be demonstrated by one of
the world's best exponents of Judo.
As an experiment which has never been tried before, the
venture is seen by Cornes & Co., as a new approach to selling.
"Many women have more tact and business ability than
men. If we find the experiment works as we think it will, more
girls will be taken on in other parts of the country," said
Leonard Steel, a director of Cornes.
- ends -

activity: Skipper DOUG EMERY of the cockle boat 'Sylvia May', using a short metal headed rake to work cockles out of the mud

te.text:
COCKLE TI ME
AT LEIGH ON SEA		DO/VIG

The humble cockle keeps the average Londoner
occupied for, at the most ten minutes, when
purchased by the saucer at the kerb-side- it keeps
the young and old of LEIGH ON SEA, busy however,
all the year round. There are other cockle grounds
around the English coasts, but Leigh claims to be
the biggest.
Leigh's fishing grounds bring out the family
boats in all seasons, and the succulent shell fish
are sieved, washed sorted and boiled, in sheds
down on the shore. The cockles are raked from
the mud at low tide, and the boats are out at the
ground, perhaps for 12 hours at a stretch.

PHOTO SHOWS:- Skipper DOUG EMERY of the cockle
boat "Sylvia May", uses a short metal headed rake to
work cockles out of the mud. It's no joke with the
cold weather coming on.
FOX PHOTOS Oct 1949 413192

WILLIAM SHAKESPEARE
LAKES PLASTIC HUMAN EYES

25 FEB 1947

The need for the human artificial eyes never has
been as heavy as now, asx the aftermath of the war
of course. Mr. William SHAKESPEARE (not the poet,
dramatist and dreamer but our contemporary, a typical
English craftsman, of Leigh-on-Sea)
has made a great step forward to relieve the world
shortage by making unbreakable plastic eyes. They
are much lighter and safer than ordinary glass eyes,
and they look perfectly natural and life-like.

eyes vary greatly in sizes, tints, one
may even say, expression. They are
fitted individually so that the
difference between the real and the
artificial eye is hardly noticeable.

activity: Smoke rising from the hull of the battleship H.M.S. Rodney during shipbreaking operations at T. Ward's scrapyard in Inverkeithing, Scotland.

te.text:
"GRAVEYARD OF GIANTS"
WHERE BATTLESHIPS GO FOR SCRAP    DG/PR

"Abandon Hope All Ye That Enter Here" is the ironic
warning over the entrance to the jetty of Messrs.
Thomas Ward, shipbreakers, of Inverkeithing,
Scotland, and so far as warships are concerned, the
phrase applies down to the last rivet.
Wards are the biggest shipbreakers in Britain, and
one of the largest in the world,  Not only are they
the biggest shipbreakers, but they break up the
biggest ships.  To their yards and to others
such as Metal Industries, or Arnott and Young's-
come such floating giants as "Rodney", "Revenge",
"Renown"; the "New York", once Hitler's "strength
through joy" liner, and many others.  Mighty fighting
ships which sailed triumphantly through two world
wars, find their last resting place under scrapyard
cranes.  Guns which the combined fleets of
the Third Reich and Imperial Japanese Navy, failed
to muzzle, are silent as hissing oxy-acetylene
cutters carve into their vitals.
Much of the valuable scrap goes to sea again in
the form of new ships, and thus fights in Britain's
export drive.  Brass, copper and much needed alloys
are sent to Sheffield, while metal scrap goes to
Newcastle.

PHOTO SHOWS:- Smoke rises in a black pall over the
hull of H.M.S. Rodney, at T. Ward's scrapyard.
Rodney has been broken up in 16 months and the
remaining oil and sludge in her double-bottoms
is burned out to continue the cutting operations.
FOX PHOTOS  MMH

THIS PHOTOGRAPH
has not been submitted
to EVENING PAPERS

activity: Miss Mollie Taylor, a glass-eye maker, blowing a piece of glass tubing into shape in a workshop.

te.text:
2442)      SHE MAKES "EYES" FOR A LIVING

A brother and sister, aged 20 and 22 respectively are
now carrying on a trade which has been in the family
for nearly a century - that of specialists in the
difficult art of making glass eyes. They are Miss
Mollie and Mr. Gus Taylor, who with the aid of a
Bunsen Burner, tubes of coloured glass, strong lungs,
and above all, artistic talent, sit in their West
End workshop supplying the demand which comes from
all over the world for their particular produce. In
addition to making glass eyes for living persons, the
Taylors make them for a number of figures at Madame
Tussauds, Mr. Gus Taylor having made the eyes for the
figure of the Duchess of Kent. A glass eye takes about
half-an-hour to make.

Photo shows :- MISS MOLLIE TAYLOR, who is the youngest
woman glass-eye maker in the world, blowing a
piece of glass tubing into shape in their West End shop.

THE OLDEST OF THEM ALL.

GK/7262-14.  The man who is not too old at 84.  John Beddow, 
has been working since he was 14 full time, before that he 
worked half time from the age of 10, earning 1/1d. a week. 
Like the other men he is now paid the basic rate for the job 
he does.  His money averages £4 a week.

THE OLD FOLK OF INDUSTRY

GK/7262.  Seeking to prove a man is "not too old at 70"
is the engineering firm of Rubery, Owen and Co. of Darlaston,
Staffs who have started an "Old Folks Workshop" which they
call "Sons of Rest".  Situated about a mile away from the
noise and bustle of the main factory, twelve men, all over
the age of 70 work on their own with no young workers beside
them to give them an inferiority complex over their ages.
The veterans start an hour later than the main factory.  They
do drilling and assembly work on office equipment and farm
implements for overseas markets.  The experiment has been
going on for 10 months and has proved a great success. Doctors
who are urging more active employment for elderly people for
the benefit of their health support it.  It is also a means
of saving for industry skilled hands vitally necessary these
days, which would otherwise be lying idle.

activity: surface at Rawdon Colliery after the container winding system had been introduced

te.text:
RAWDON COLLIERY.

Rawdon Colliery, which is on the border of
Derbyshire and Leicestershire, is now one of the most
efficient collieries in the country. Before 1952
success in improving output had reached a stage where it
was not possible to get more coal out of the pit without
reorganising the shafts for higher capacity. An
entirely new method of overcoming this difficulty, whilst
avoiding delays and consequent loss of output, was
conceived by the former Area General Manager,
Mr. J.J.Torrance, and his Chief Engineer, Mr. F.Ashley.
They scrapped all the complicated and orthodox methods
of collecting the coal and installed an automatic system
employing six movable containers, each holding 4 tons,
to replace tubs used for winding up the shaft. These
containers, which are moved on rollers in and out of the
winding cage, are filled from a bunker at pit-bottom, and
are wound and emptied at high speed, only one man con-
trolling the operation on the surface.

Winding now takes place in one shaft instead of two,
and the six containers replace 650 tubs formerly used for
winding the output up the shafts.

The reorganisation has reduced the number of men
employed from 114 to 16, and improved the capacity of the
Rawdon shaft from 148 to 360 tons an hour

CROWN COPYRIGHT RESERVED.  MINISTRY OF HOUSING & LOCAL GOVERNMENT.
Four prototype houses built for the Sheffield City Council by the
Public Works Department under the 5M system of construction devised
by the Research and Development Group of the Ministry of Housing
and Local Government.  This system, which marks a new attempt to
bring the advantages of industrialisation into the field of house-
building, has been derived from the 5M CLASP system used at
Stevenage for a group of old people's flatlets.  The new system
is called 5M, because as at Stevenage, it is based upon a planning
grid of 1' 8" (5 x the module of 4").  The object has been to
modify the CLASP system which has been shown to have advantages in
the reduction of site labour and building time, to suit the
performance standards, and the levels of cost, of 2-storey housing.

Ministry of Housing & Local Government.           January, 1963

te.text:
CALCRAFT   ILLUS.                 8.12.42
SADLER'S WELLS BALLET
The present season at the New Theatre ends on
December 19th. The company then go to York (Theatre
Royal) where they open on Christmas Eve. They go on
to the Prince's Theatre, Bradford, from January 4th
to 9th, and after a holiday, return to the New
Theatre on January 25th.
THE BIRDS
The choregrapher is Robert Helpmann, who has set this
his third ballet to the music of Respighi. The
detting and dresses are by a Chinese artist, Chiang Yee.
The ballet was first presented at the New Theatre on
November 24th, and will be in the repertoire of the
Company when they are in Yorkshire.
THE SYNOPSIS
There is no bird in the garden that pleases the
melancholy Dove, least of all the Hen who makes
ludicrous advances to him. Not until he meets the
simple Nightingale does he fall in love. Unfortunately
his feelings are shared by the jealous and pompous
Cuckoo (who has quarrelled with both the hen and the
Sparrows). In a despairing effort to gain their
amours, the Cuckoo disguises himself as the Dove, while
the Hen disguises herself as the Nightingale. No
one is deceived by the disguise except the two
impostors, who fall happily into each other's arms.
But they are quickly unmasked by the mischievous
Sparrows. They leave after an angry scene and the
Sparrows prepare the way for the wedding of the Dove
and the Nightingale.
1. The Dove (Alexis Rasine) and the Nightingale
(Beryl Grey).

activity: casual workers picking radishes in the rain under mobile steel skeleton tents called 'igloos' on a farm

te.text:
"IGLOOS" ON A KENT FARM

Fourteen "IGLOOS" - small tents constructed
with a rigid tubular steel skeleton, have made their
appearance at TEMPLE FARM, DARTFORD MARSHES, KENT.
This is from an idea of the farmer - MR. FRED
BARKER, and it now enables his workers, both casual and
regular, to work even in the bad weather.
Normally, when it rains and there is no
inside work most workers are "stood off". On MR. BARKER'S
farm there is now full employment at all times.
It also helps him to get his crops picked
at the right time. For instance, radishes must come out
not a day later than three weeks after sowing.
PICTURE SHOWS:

CASUAL WORKERS PICKING RADISHES
IN THE RAIN THIS MORNING. WHEN
HOEING, THE CONTRAPTION IS LIFTED
AND DRAGGED AFTER THEM. FRONT
FORKS ARE PUSHED INTO THE GROUND FOR
STABILITY IN WIND.
56625 4/6/56 JOHN TOPHAM

TOPHAM, LTD.
20, MAIN ROAD,
SIDCUP,
KENT.
FOOTS CRAY 2116 - DAY & NIGHT

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
- 5 JUN 1956
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

te.text:
AN ILLUSTRATION from
THE DAILY MAIL IDEAL HOME EXHIBITION
OLYMPIA, MARCH 6—MARCH 31 1962
WITH COMPLIMENTS—NO FEE is required for reproduction of this picture if it is published as news
of THE IDEAL HOME EXHIBITION at Olympia, or in conjunction with an article about this exhibition
PATRICK MURPHY, The Press Representative.

6195
The vast space of the Grand Hall, permeated with light and warmth, is a repre-
sentation of a Caribbean settlement by the sea. From the entrance, visitors
will see the House in the Sun, a beautiful white modern structure which is
both a suntrap and sun shield. From the "hills" behind a waterfall passes
beneath the house before sliding away. The interior of the House is as
beguiling as its outward appearance. The living room is furnished to the
tastes of Sir Malcolm Sargent; the electronic bedroom by Stirling Moss and
the kitchen by Mrs. John Profumo - actress Valerie Hobson. Approaching this
House from the Main Entrance, visitors will pass through lines of colourful
stands garlanded with flowers. Towering 50 ft. above the stands, four Apamate
trees fill the vast space with their huge canopies of variegated foliage.
O.P.S. The bedroom designed by Stirling Moss. Entirely electronic, it is
modelled on the bedroom he is building for himself in his new home in
Shepherds Market.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
- 6 MAR 1962
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

The prototype of a new system of industrialised house
building has just been completed by Housing Development &
Construction Ltd., at Stratford-upon-Avon. It is a pair of
semi-detached, three bedroomed houses, designed and built to
the full Parker-Morris Committee Recommendations, and to the
specification of the local authority Stratford-upon-Avon M.B.
It only required three weeks of normal working with a very
small team of men to complete this pair of houses for occupation.
This is undoubtedly the fastest erection time of any system
of truly permanent housing for local authorities yet developed.
The 16 ft. x 12 ft. living room of the centrally heated
H.D.C. house is separated from the dining and kitchen
area by a glazed screen - just one of several alternatives.
All walls and ceiling have an unusually high degree of heat
insulation.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
20 SEP 1963

 ... Even then firemen, police and

 they were sure all the playmates 
 were safe.

te.text:
166182 LUD
AMERICA IMPORTING BRITISH-MADE FERGUSON TRACTORS.
£15,000,000 ORDER.
Coventry, Eng: In the world's largest tractor factory
operated by multi-millionaire Harry Ferguson here,
250 tractors leave the production lines every day as
part of a £15,000,000 order for America - one of the
greatest manufacturers of these machines.
First batch of this order - vital part of Britain's
export drive - will sail in the freighter 'American
Farmer', recently salvaged off British coasts when
sailing here with essential parts for the tractors.
The machines, selling to the States at £372 each, are
made at the Coventry plant leased by the 63-year-old
Ferguson, who recently returned from America to live
at his Cotswold home.
PHOTO SHOWS: Newly-completed Ferguson tractors are
driven to their place in the 'export line' -
machines waiting shipment to America at the Coventry
factory.
January 16th 1948 PN.g. List 1.

TURNING GOLD INTO BOOKS.

In spite of thousands of years of scientific research
a machine has not yet been invented to beat gold, with
the delicate manipulation which is essential to success,
and so the job is still carried on by hand, in almost
the same way as it was carried on in the time of Queen
Cleopatra, varying only in the fact that  a bronze hammer
was used by the ancients in place of the steel one used
today, and that machinery forms a small part of the
early stages..
O.P.S.  Gold beaters at work, for hours on end these
        men beat away with their hammers until the
        squares and ribbons of gold are in leaves, only
        four millionth of an inch in thickness.
        JS/P    Keystone.

te.text:
D.H. White.           5.11.47.

Fishing for coal in the Leeds-Liverpool
canal at Adlington, Lancs. (See story).

19. Robert Davis hands in his home made
    cage with coal in.

FISHING FOR COAL IN THE LEEDS-LIVERPOOL, CANAL.
The Leeds-Liverpool canal at Chorley, Lancs,
is almost dry-just a little water in the middle
of masses of mud.
Seventy-three-years-old Jimmy Blundell, who sailed
that canal as captain of the barge for almost 50
years and his pal Bob Davis, aged 66, another ex-barge
skipper, remembered that coal fell out of the barges
into the canal.
So Jimmy and Bob made a metal dredge. It pulls up
broken bottles and stones but coal too.
The two ex-captains are working their way along the
canal and average two bags of coal every afternoon.
OPS. Robert Davis hands in his home made cage with
coal in.

te.text: g a silk stocking length as it leaves the

Making Silk Stockings.
In an old workhouse which has been converted
into a factory, between 25,000 and 30,000 dozen
pairs of nylon, pure silk and rayon stockings
are being produced each week.
Most of the stockings made in this factory are
non-fashioned. They are made on a circular
machine and the mock fashioning marks and seams
are added after they come off.
Fully fashioned stockings are knitted flat and seams
are joined afterwards.
The entire output of fully fashioned nylon stockings
and a considerable quantity of mock fashioned
stockings made in this factory are all for
export.

OPS. The stockings are put on to a moving belt of flat
metal "legs" to be shaped before it is sprayed with
water.

activity: Massey-Harris No.21, 12 foot cut combine harvester gathering wheat on land formerly requisitioned for military use

te.text:
The rapid expansion of allied air forces during the war resulted in
aerodromes sprawling across some of Britain's best agricultural land.  When
the planes finally departed, this requisitioned land, covered with runways,
perimeter tracks and military installations, was left neglected.

Co-Partnership Farms Ltd of Boreham, Essex, lost some of their best
land in this way and it was only recently handed back to them.  They immed-
iately commenced clearing all traces of military occupation so that the land
could be prepared for cropping as soon as possible.

The results of this work can be seen in the picture which shows a
Massey-Harris No.21, 12 foot cut combine harvester gathering wheat at one
hundred quarters a day from two hundred and seventy acres of land that had been
under military occupation for more than six years.

It is essential under present conditions that all land be brought back
into production as quickly as possible.  It says much for individual industry
that not only has it brought this war neglected land back into good heart, but
is using the most modern means to harvest the crops which are the result of
their initiative and labour.


Co-Partnership Farms Ltd
Boreham,           Chelmsford
(No Fee or Acknowledgement required)

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE 
'DAILY HERALD' ART LIBRARY 
AND MUST BE RETURNED 
UNDAMAGED

te.text:
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
16 OCT 1958
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

Friends restrain one of the
caravan dwellers. The
[illegible]
are seen centre one wearing a mac
the other wearing a homberg

Two bailiffs—in homburg and coat—are forced back.
72 FAMILIES
FORCE OUT
THE BAILIFFS
FOUR bailiffs who went to
clear 72 families from
their homes on a caravan site
had to retreat yesterday be-
fore they could serve one
eviction notice.
A mass of angry men and
women linked arms and forced
the bailiffs off the site.
Then the caravaners blocked
entrances to the site with an old
caravan and two old cars.
Today they will be ready to
carry on the fight for their
homes.
The families live in Chertsey-
lane, Egham, Surrey. The local
council has told them they must
go because the site is in the
Green Belt area. An extension
of their notice-to-quite ended
yesterday.
A TRUCE
When the bailiffs first arrived
a two-hour "truce" was agreed
while a deputation from the
site went to No. 10, Downing-
street.
They were told the Prime
Minister could not intervene. At
the Ministry of Housing they
got the same answer.
The deputation returned and
the bailiffs tried to move in.
Within ten minutes they were
back on the road.
They told the caravaners:
" We will be back."
The families have been offered
temporary accommodation and
later Army huts as homes in
Godalming. But they refuse to
leave...

activity: sections of the first Canadian ship are assembled together in a large new workshop at a shipyard dry dock in Newport

te.text:
PROPERTY OF 
 DAILY HERALD 
 RCD. 18 FEB 1954 
 PLEASE RETURN 
 TO 
 ART LIBRARY

LONDON BUREAU 
 LN 266266 DAW 
 SHIP BEING BUILT IN UNFINISHED DRY DOCK 
 UNDER-COVER BUILDING 
 NEWPORT, MON: The first British shipyard in 
 which vessels are being built in dry dock and 
 under cover is somewhat unique in that work 
 is being carried out on the first of two 3,000 
 ton ships while the dock itself is in the process 
 of construction. Thus, as the size of the ship 
 grows, so will the dock. If everything goes 
 according to plan, they will, by the time the ship 
 is built, be able to open the dock gate and allow 
 the vessel to float out on the 40 ft. tide. 
 The dock, which was opened in November by 
 Sir David Maxwell Fyfe, Home Secretary and Minister 
 for Welsh Affairs, is situated at the mouth of the 
 River Usk. The two ships ordered are both wood 
 pulp carriers for a Canadian company, and sections 
 of them, after being prefabricated in a number of 
 shops, are lowered into position in the dock. 
 PHOTO SHOWS:- In the large new workshop at the dock, 
 sections of the first Canadian ship are assembled 
 together. 
 17th February 1954 PN-b

Indus Shipbuilding Yards etc 
 x ref

activity: the features and development of the Gillette Techmatic razor

te.text:
SOME THINGS, like raw gold and racehorses, improve with handling. The
same isn't true of razor blades. In fact, the more you handle a blade, the
tougher your shaving task is likely to become. Even removing it carelessly
from the paper wrapper can badly bruise the cutting edge.
Which is why those mag-
nificent men who design
shaving machines have at
last come up with a super-
swift invention that does
away with the need for any-
one ever to touch a razor
blade again.
The new Techmatic razor,
developed by Gillette, offers all
the close-shave advantages of
the traditional razor while
eliminating completely the
chore of gingerly switching
blades.
Like all the best inventions,
the idea behind it is a simple
one, similar to the cartridge-
loading of a camera.
FLICK
In effect, the Techmatic
presents the shaver with a
slender 10in.-long razor blade,
safely coiled inside a plastic
clip-on cartridge.
The actual length of shaving
edge exposed to the chin is the
same as in the normal razor.
But as the edge becomes dulled
you merely flick a lever to wind
in the next razor-sharp section.
A numbered window at the
back of the razor tells you how
many edges you have used up,
and since the coil is irrever-
sible there is no danger of
going back to a previously used
edge.
When the entire 10in. coil
has been wound through the
streamlined razor-head you buy
a new clip-on cartridge and
start again.
At the moment, unless you
live in the London television
area, the Techmatic is a
machine that money can't buy.
The razor, which sells at £2 2s.,
has been given a highly suc-
cessful trial run in the capital,
where the refill cartridges are
now available at 8s. 11d. each.
'The Techmatic will be
by WILLIAM SPICER
introduced nationwide. We
anticipate a heavy demand
since the Techmatic is the
very last word in shaving com-
fort,' says Vivian Burchill,
group brand manager.
'We reckon that the aver-
age shaver will only need to
buy new Techmatic cartridges
four or five times a year. One
Techmatic edge lasts as long as
a double-edged blade.'
Perhaps the big break-
through that really short-
circuited the electric shaver
men was the discovery that
stainless-steel razor blades
could be vastly improved by
giving them a coating of very
special plastic.
This process, invented and
patented by Gillette, has re-
moved the drag from shaving.
SLICE
'Imagine the bristles on
your chin as small saplings
and the razor blade as an axe,'
says Peter Williams, Gillette's
head of development.
'In the old days, the axe
would cut half-way through
each sapling and then have to
be tugged the rest of the way.
In some mysterious way, the
new plastic coating enables the
blade to slice through sapling
after sapling with absolutely
no sign of tug. We know what
it does, but I have to admit
that we don't yet understand
how.'
The miracle coating—a solid
fluorocarbon polymer similar
to the chemical applied to non-
stick frying pans—stubbornly
refuses to give up its secrets.
'You might call it a lucky
discovery,' says Peter Williams.
'But it came as the result of
painstaking research.'
Gillette have mastered the
secret of making this micro-
scopically thin film behave on
the edge of their Super Silver
blades. And naturally the
technique is thrown in as an
'extra' with the new con-
veyor-belt Techmatic.

Paddington Green Children's Hospital has carried on
throughout the war and during the 1940-41 Blitz many
nerve-racked children were treated by the Hospital
and were sent to the country during convalescence.

patients under their wing and having made toys for
all the children they acted nursery rhymes and sang

      in Nursery Rhymes clothes.

activity: Mrs. Cropp and children at the door of their "home", a wooden fruit picker's hut on Wested Farm.

te.text:
PROBLEM OF A WOMAN AND SIX CHILDREN
---
Living in one room - a wooden fruit picker's
hut, on Wested Farm, Crockenhill, near Swanley,
Kent, is Mrs. May Cropp, her three children and a
further three granchildren (offspring of one of her
daughters).
She is a squatter.  There is no sanitation
anywhere near the hut - nor the usual amenites.  The
hut leaks, is unsanitary, and is certainly not
weatherproof.
How she came to be there does not matter - what
does matter is that she cannot get another home to
live - and owing to the bad state of affairs the
farmer, C.T. Miller, of Wested Farm, has asked the
police to evict them in the hope that they will
be found better accomodation.
As it is, the children - ranging from a few
months to six years - cannot possibly be properly
fed, clothed and educated - and there is no talk of
them going regularly to school.
In this cold weather, some of them are to
be seen playing in the mud around their "home".
The Dartford Rural District Council, under
whose jurisdiction their "home" comes, should look
into the matter - the farmer is certainly not to
[illegible] the best housing he can offer - even
2.  Mrs. Cropp and children at the door of their
"home".
19836      4/12/46      John Topham, Sidcup, Kent.

Dec 19th 1966 PAP 125712-1 (PNR-G)

AMERICA ORDERS MORE JETSTREAMS

The first prototype HP 137 JETSTREAM, an
executive and local-service aircraft,
under construction at the Handley Page
works at Radlett, Hertfordshire.
Now, five months before the plane's first
flight, it is announced that America has
placed an order for an additional 65

have been ordered by K.R. Cravens Corporation
of St. Louis, Missouri, through its wholly-
owned subsidiary International Jetstream

order placed earlier this year.
Jetstreams, powered by prop-jet engines, are
able to use small grass fields, cruise at
over 300 mph, fly at 30,000 ft., and have
a range of 2,000 miles.
The first prototype is due to fly next Spring.

activity: Angry villagers demanding the demolition of a new block of council flats in Croft, Leicestershire, which they describe as looking like a prison.

te.text:
ANGRY VILLAGERS are to demand that a new block of 
council flats should be pulled down. They claim the block 
looks just like a prison. 
“It’s an absolute monstrosity,” one villager said 
last night. “If a private builder dared to build 
such a thing the council would be the first to 
object.” 
The £30,000 flats at 
Croft, Leics, are being 
built of concrete sections. 
Work on them is almost 
finished. 
But the villagers want all 
work on the “prison” to stop. 
Their parish council have 
asked Blaby Rural Council to 
meet a village deputation as 
soon as possible to hear 
demands for the demolition 
of the building. 
EYESORE 
Yesterday Mr. Don Wood, 
who lives opposite the flats 
in Broughton Road, Croft, 
said: “If the council had set 
out to create an eyesore 
deliberately they could not 
have done a better job.” 
Another Broughton Road 
resident, Mr. Ian Woollard, 
declared: “If we fail to get 
satisfaction we shall go to 
the Ministry of Housing and 
Local Government.” 
His neighbour, Mr. Charles 
Saxton, added: “Someone 
has made an almighty mis- 
take in putting up this mon- 
strosity. It must come 
down.” 
Mr. Thomas Heap, Clerk of 
Blaby Rural Council, said: 
“These are the first flats of 
this type we have erected. 
We didn’t expect this 
uproar.”

SUN 
 PROPERTY 
 15 JUL 1966 
 Please return to 
 ART LIBRARY
