activity: oil-burning boilers at the new Bankside Power Station starting to supply electricity.

te.text:
244479         SKI
BANKSIDE POWER STATION STARTS PRODUCTION.

London:    A battery of 12 oil-burning boilers at
the new and controversial Bankside Power Station,
at which the first 60,000-kilowatt turbo-alternator,
of about 80,000 horse-power, has just started to
supply electricity.
One of the conditions under which the power station
was allowed laid down that oil and not coal was to
be burned. Other conditions were that the building
was approved by the Royal Fine Arts Commission, and
that the building must be set back far enough from
the Thames not to interfere with the projected road
and promenade. The protests about the building
came from the London County Council, the City Council,
and the Southwark Council, from the Dean and
Chapter of St. Paul's Cathedral - the planned power
station was opposite to St. Paul's, on the other side
of the river - and from such bodies as the Society
for the Protection of Ancient Buildings. Opposition
became so strong that in January 1947 a public
inquiry was held. The Government, however, allowed
the building, provided that the conditions were
observed.
When completed the station will comprise four
60,000-kilowatt generating sets, when the oil
consumption at full load, 16-hours a day, will be 67
tons an hour, consuming (in one winter's day) about
850 tons.
January 20th. 1953.   PN-h

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
21 JAN 1953
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

FILE - INDUSTRY - FUEL & POWER,
ELECTRICITY, Power Stations

activity: discovery of the body of a deceased male infant on a railway line

te.text:
At 6.25a.m. on 27th May, the dead body of a baby
boy aged about 1 month, well nourished was found
on the Southern Railway line between Barnes
Common and Putney.
The body was clad in a white knitted vest. There
were many injuries to the body, and burns as a result
of coming into [crossed out] contact with the conductor
rail, which suggests it had been thrown from a
train proceeding towards Waterloo. The child was
well developed, with fair hair and blue eyes.
The police are anxious to trace any person
travelling between Barnes and Putney between 9.30
and 1 a.m. 27th May, who might have seen anything
dropped from a carriage window, or who has any
knowledge of a male child of his age being missing
from its accustomed place.

Mrs MARGUERITE EASTWOOD (committed)
sentenced to death for the
murder of the baby.

MANNEQUIN AND FURS.

Commonwealth and fashioned in London by the British Fur

to the value of many hundreds of pounds.

Ocelot trimmed with Nutria.

activity: A farm worker and his employer chatting over a garden gate in front of a newly built house.

te.text:
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
EDITORIAL
LIBRARY

The house
that LEONARD
built ...
FARM-WORKER Leonard
Algar claims a housing
record of his own.
In the little village of Carl-
ton Colville, near Lowestoft,
stands a well-built house, with
three bedrooms, three rooms
downstairs, bathroom, elec-
tricity, hot and cold water, and
three-quarters of an acre of
garden.
Built more than fourteen
months ago, this house is be-
lieved to be the first to be
erected under the Govern-
ment's scheme which helps
farm workers to have houses
built for themselves on their
own land.
His employer, Farmer Stan-
ley Newson, of Grove Farm,
told me about it. "Leonard
bought the land, had the house
built, and got married," he
said. "I think a lot of farm
workers would do the same if
they knew that the facilities
were available."
What are these facilities?
Up to 85 per cent. of the total
cost of building a house can be
borrowed at the rate of 3 1/2 per
cent. interest, repayable within
30 years.
For example, if the house
cost £1,100 (the price Leonard
paid for his) as much as £935
could be borrowed, if necessary.
The cost of interest and re-
payment over this period would
then average less than £1 per
week, and less still, of course,
if the sum borrowed were
smaller.
The scheme also provides an
annual grant, increased by the
Labour Government to £15 for
40 years, a total of £600, for all
such houses occupied by farm
workers.
And no development charges
are made where these houses
are concerned.
The first step for a farm
worker to take is to apply to
the clerk of his rural district
council. Those councils that
administer the Small Dwellings
Acquisition Act, which deals
with this matter, should pro-
perly give priority in the grant-
ing of building licences to men
working on the land.
The farm worker who is a
member will find that his
union is always ready to help
him deal with the formalities.
B. A. Steward
The kitchen—light, modern,
well-equipped.
Over their own front gate the
Algars chat with Farmer
Newson.

activity: An official from the St Pancras Housing department posting requisitioning notices on the door of No. 5 Houghton Place.

te.text:
Mr. O'LEARY WINS HIS HOME BACK
" Herald " Reporter
HERE is the cameraman's view of the closing stages of the Battle of the Second Floor Back, which ended yesterday at Houghton-place, N.W., in victory for the tenant.
The battle began six weeks ago when Mr. Charles O'Leary was evicted from the single room sublet to him by Mrs. Eliades after a Tribunal had reduced his rent from £2 10s. to 17s. 6d.
Three days ago St. Pancras Borough Council requisitioned the room—but a new lock on the street door kept Mr. O'Leary and his wife out.
So the Town Clerk, acting under the powers recently given by Mr. Bevan, requisitioned the whole house.
When Mr. O'Leary and council officials went along yesterday to take possession they found the front door open—but there was a new lock on the door of his flat.
" Break it open," said the Housing Manager to the council's joiner—and here you see him doing it, with Mr. O'Leary looking on. The other picture shows an official posting up the requisitioning notice.
Within a few minutes the lock had been replaced by another and two keys given to Mr. O'Leary.
Said the Housing Manager: " I'm notifying Mrs. Eliades that she and her tenants are now our tenants; that she now has no right to deny any tenant access to this house and that she must obey the Council."
Mr. O'Leary says he is suing Mrs. Eliades for loss of six weeks' wages—" about £60."
" I'd to give up my job as a chef to take time off to fight this case," he told me. " I've been separated from my wife, who had to take a ' sleeping-in ' job in a hospital and I have had to sleep in lodging-houses. For a few days after we were turned out we had to live in a work-house."

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

activity: Norman Cornish, a coal hewer and artist, standing with his portrait of his grandmother at the 'Art by the Miner' exhibition at the Academy Cinema.

te.text:
THE "OTHER LIFE"
OF NORMAN
CORNISH, MINER
SINCE he was 14, Norman
Cornish—he is only 28
now—has led two lives.
One has been spent in the
Dean and Chapter Colliery,
Durham, where he earns his
living as a coal-hewer.
The other has been spent with
brushes and canvas in his free
time, recording with steadily in-
creasing mastery of form and
colour the men and the women
and the grim grandeur of the
world of coal.
And now, along with other
miners who fill their leisure time
with the colour they never see at
work, he is exhibiting his paint-
ings in London.
Norman was taught to draw
and paint at the Spennymoor
Settlement. Five of his paint-
ings in the present exhibition
have been bought by the Na-
tional Coal Board, which
sponsors the show.
Outstanding is his portrait of
his grandmother—he is standing
by it in this "Daily Herald"
photograph. "She's grand," he
says.
This exhibition covers many
artistic activities besides paint-
ing. There are ship models,
carvings, model aircraft, work-
ing models of mines, violins,
pipes, table-linen and shawls. .
"Art and the Miner" is on
view at the Academy Cinema,
Oxford-street, W. It opens today
from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. (Sundays
2 p.m. to 10 p.m.) and closes
November 2. Admission is free.

Copyright
Photo
BY F. GREAVES.

N.S. Cornish a coal hewer from Dean and Chapter
colliery Durham with a painting of his grandmother
which is exhibited at the Art by the Miner exhibition
which opened at the Academy Cinema today.

VAST YARDS OF THE FAMOUS BUILDERS, VICKERS ARMSTRONG, BARROW-
IN-FURNESS, SHE IS DUE TO BE LAUNCHED THIS AUTUMN AND WHEN COM-
PLETED WILL TAKE UP SERVICE ON THE AUSTRALIA AND PACIFIC RUN IN
CONJUNCTION WITH THE P & O LINER "CANBERRA", ALSO OF 40,000 TONS,
WHICH IS TO BE LAUNCHED A FEW MONTHS AFTER THE "ORIANA".
IT HAS BEEN CLAIMED THAT THERE IS MORE ALUMINIUM BEING USED IN
CONSTRUCTION OF THE ORIANA THAN WAS USED IN THE PRIDE OF AMERICA'S
SHIPPING WORLD, FLAG-SHIP OF THE UNITED STATES LINE, THE C
53,000 TONNER, "UNITED STATES". THE REASON FOR THIS IS THAT PRE-
VIOUSLY WHERE ALUMINIUM HAS BEEN USED TO ANY GREAT DEGREE, STEEL
STIFFENERS HAVE BEEN ESSENTIAL TO HELP WITH THE INTEGRAL RIGIDITY
REQUIRED IN THE CONSTRUCTION OF A LARGE SHIP OF PRESENT-DAY STAN-
DARDS.
THE ALUMINIUM SUPERSTRUCTURE WEIGHING JUST OVER 1,000 TONS, COM-
PRISES FIVE DECKS, TWO BRIDGE DECKS, AND ALL UPPER WORKS. THE
TOTAL AREA OF BULKHEAD AND DECK PLATING OF THIS MATERIAL IS ALMOST
350,000 SQ FT.
ABOUT 90% OF THE SUPERSTRUCTURE [struck through text] HAS BEEN ASSEMBLE
IN A PREFABRICATED FORM IN SHOPS ENTIRELY INDEPENDENT OF THE MAIN
YARDS.
THE COST OF THIS GIANT NEW SHIP, THE LARGEST PASSENGER VESSEL TO
BE CONSTRUCTED IN THIS COUNTRY SINCE THE ALL-TIME RECORD BREAKER,
"QUEEN ELIZABETH", 83,673 TONS, IS £12 1/2 M.
A MOST INTERESTING FEATURE OF THIS BEAUTIFUL NEW SHIP IS THE BULBOUS
FOREFOOT, THIS, IT APPEARS, ENABLES THE SHIP TO TRAVEL AT A VERY
MUCH HIGHER SPEED WITHOUT THE ADDED EXPENSE OF EXTRA POWER. A
FEATURE WHICH WILL NO DOUBT BE INCORPORATED IN MANY FUTURE BRITISH
SHIPS.
THIS PICTURE, TAKEN RECENTLY IN THE YARDS OF VICKERS ARMSTRONG,
SHOWS

A VIEW FROM THE STERN OF THE ORIANA SHOWING PLAINLY THE ALUMINIUM
SUPERSTRUCTURE BEGINNING TO RISE FROM THE STEEL HULL.

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION THURSDAY'S EVENINGS, July 24th.,

SILK WORMS THAT HELP BRITAIN'S EXPORTS
24.7.47.
A small but very important aid to British export trade is
being given by about six million silk worms which are being
reared at Lullingstone Castle Silk Farm, run by ZOE, LADY
HART DYKE, near Eynsford, Kent. The aim and object of the
farm, which is now getting going again after the war, is to
develop and assist production of raw silk in this country, the
Dominions, and the Colonies, and what started off as a girl's
hobby, developed on a business footing in 1932, is now a
flourishing industry housed in one of Britain's ancient homes.
The Lullingstone silkworms are known all over the world for
millions of them have been exported, and it was from their silk
that the Coronation Robes for the Queen and the Princesses
were made. One of the difficulties at present being ex-
perienced is the lack of mulberry leaves on which to feed
the worms, for the eighteen acre plantation at Lullingstone
is only producing about half the number of leaves required
to feed six million tiny mouths.
It is interesting to note that the method of using the silk
cocoon for spinning and weaving was first known in China at
least 3,000 years B.C. It was James I who endeavoured to
encourage silk worm rearing in this country by ordering the
importation and planting of thousands of mulberry trees, but
the Royal scheme was a failure. George I then took a keen
interest in the silk industry and in 1718 he granted a
patent to a certain John Appleton for silkworm rearing.
The picture shows a gleaming skein of raw silk being
tested layer by layer for any break s or flaws before it
is weighed and pressed for dispatching to the throwster and
weavers.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

GIANT WINDMILL TO TEST POWER THEORY 29.6.53.
Going up today at Prae Wood, St. Albans, is a 100 kilo-
watt generator, part of a 100 ft tower which is to be
built with giant windmill blades on top to test
the efficiency of getting electric power in a big
scale from the wind. On the success of this experiment

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY'S EVENINGS JULY 27th.

TIMBER AS A MUNITION OF WAR.
CANADIAN LUMBERJACKS IN BRITAIN SAVE SHIPPING SPACE.
27.7.42.
Vast quantities of timber are needed in wartime. Vital
shipping space is, however, saved for other necessities
by the efforts of the Canadian Forestry Corps. These
skilled, hardy men, who come from all parst of the
great Dominion and who are soldiers too, have established

Dan Michaud of Grand Falls, New Brunswick, is typical

activity: horses waiting to be shod outside the roadside blacksmith's forge

te.text:
A RARE SIGHT IN THIS MODERN AGE. MJH/H.3.

In this modern age, the once familiar sight of the
village blacksmith, is now becoming very rare as
machinery replaces horses on the farm. In some
districts, however, where hilly land makes machinery
unpracticable, horses are still in use and the smith
is still very necessary. One such area is the Lake District
where blacksmiths can still be seen at work in their
old stone forges.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: A scene which is now becoming rare
is this one of horses waiting to be shod outside
the roadside blacksmith's forge at Crosthwaite, near
Windermere, Westmorland.

te.text:
E.M./HT.

THATCHING MACHINE HELPS ON THE FARM.

A machine invented and patented nearly half-a-century ago,
but never used, is now helping to solve labour problems on
British farms. It makes thatches for ricks at half the
cost and in a fifth of the time of the old hand method.
The matting can be made at any time by this machine and
can be stored in rolls till harvest time, so that ricks
can be immediately thatched to cut out risk of damage by
weather. These pictures, taken in Surrey, show the new
thatching machine in use.

Photo shows:- Miss Eleen Laxton, who was a dressmaker
before joining the Land Army, finds the work of stitching
thatch mats a familiar job.
FOX. 24th August, 1942. 279775.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION THURSDAY'S EVENS, 3.6.48.

VITAL TO THE SUCCESS OF THE AFRICAN GROUNDNUT SCHEME.
Mac 3.6.48.
The movement of the groundnuts crop in Nigeria is
being held up through lack of sufficient rolling stock.
About half the 1947/8 crop of 250,000 tons up country
will still be awaiting transport when the new crop begins
to move in the Autumn. The urgency of the new locos to
replace those worn out ones now operating is vital ; all
haste is being made in production at the Vulcan Foundry
at Newton-le-Willows (Lancs) and additionally to the 20
already sent, another 42 are expected to go during the
year. The picture shows
a completed loco undergoing the final test in steam on
a set of rollers to try out the bearings and check valves.
They are of about 70 tons, with a guage of 3ft. 6ins.

COPYRIGHT PHOTO ISSUED BY
CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
INCORPORATING
Central News Illustrations Service,

te.text:
CRAFT "IN CHARACTER".                          MJH/HT.

"When the famous Cathedral Weaving Centre of Canterbury recently
took over an old building in Best Lane (Canterbury) as an
extension to their teaching facilities, they did not know
just how appropriate it was.  However, during alterations
the casing round the main chimney of the building was removed
and workmen discovered parts of centuries old looms and spinning
wheels.  This, combined with the strength of the first storey
floors proved that it had once been a weaving establishment
and it has been ascertained that this building is the place
where the Huguenot and Walloon weavers of the Middle Ages carried
on their art of weaving when they fled from the Continent, so the
present-day weavers have the right atmosphere for their craft.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:  In the old Huguenot Centre, which has been
taken over by the Canterbury Weaving Centre, two young [illegible] girls
are seen working in the exact spot where the Huguenot and
Walloon weavers worked centuries ago.  On the left MISS MARGARET
WELLS of Faversham (Kent) is carding, whilst MISS DORIS BAILEY
sits at the spinning wheel on the original platform beneath
the eaves of the roof.

HELPING THE RE-ARMAMENT PROGRAMME.                                  CH/AT

At a wharf near Greenwich two brothers, Charles and Alfred 
Robinson, are helping on the re-armament programme. They are 
probably the biggest of London's scrap metal merchants. Most 
of the scrap comes to them in pony carts and consists of 
dilapidated iron bedsteads, old perambulators, etc, collected 
by the smaller dealers. An interesting point is the absence 
of a magnetic crane to raise loads to waiting ships. They 
are too close to Greenwich Observatory and not allowed to 
have one.

Photo shows-  Loading a boat with scrap iron for South Wales 
for making armaments.
Fox May 18th. 37.

THE SHAPE OF THINGS TO COME. MJH/RS. 
Hugh Pope, one of the assistant architects working on the 
new Coventry Cathedral, has built himself an experimental 
studio in the grounds of his home on Kingston Hill (Surrey), 
made entirely of glass with a light timber frame. The interior 
is lined with panels which can be taken out or put in, to 
suit the weather and lighting wanted. The actual frame of 
150 separate triangles was put up by Mr. Pope, his wife Jennie 
and a friends, artist Peter Kermode, over a weekend "Though I 
confess", he adds, "that the foundations and glazing were done 
by a building firm to my design. I believe that there will 
be many houses and religious buildings constructed in this way 
in the future". (THIS CAPTION MUST NOT BE ALTERED). 

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: MRS. JENNIE POPE, seen taking a vase 
of flowers into the glass studio, which her husband has 
built in the grounds of their home at Kingston Hill (Surrey).

te.text:
FRIDAY'S
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION THURSDAY'S DAILIES, March 19th.

AN UNDERWATER SEARCH FOR OIL IN GAMBIA
                                      9.3.56.
The British Petroleum Company's prospecting subsidiary,
D'Arcy Exploration Company, is now searching for oil in
Gambia, the British Colony and Protectorate on the West
coast of Africa. As a first step, a waterborne seismic
survey or more than 200 miles of the River Gambia has
begun. This is being conducted from the "SONIC", a
former landing craft, which has carried out similar work
in the Persian Gulf. The seismic survey will provide useful
information not only on the rock structure beneath the
river bed, but also on that below the neighbouring land.
It is a quicker method of making a preliminary survey than
a similar operation on land, since dense forests fringe
the River Gambia. Seismic surveys ascertain the shape of
subterranean rock structures by recording on delicate
instruments, the vibrations set up by explosive charges
fired either underground or under water.
      The picture shows a "depth-charge" like explosion
in the seaward approaches of the river Gambia after a
charge had been dropped overboard from the "Sonic".

 HARVESTING IN MAY. 
 
 Rye Harvesting, peculiar to a few parts of Gloucestershire is now

 Bristol, Glos. The seed is sown in August and harvested in May.

hundreds of cars are now being broken up.

NIGHT HARVEST.                             MJH/MAE.

Farmers all over the country have, this year, experienced
great difficulty in completing their harvesting programme,
due to the frequent wet weather. They have been forced to
do their harvesting an hour or two at a time, whenever the
weather permitted. One Gloucestershire farmer, Major
J. Bradish-Ellanes of Haymes Farm, Cleeve Hill decided to
make the most of a recent fine day by continuing with his
harvesting by night until it was finished. This was
accomplished by the use of a Combine fitted with headlights.

Bradish-Ellanes', Haymes Farm, Cleeve Hill (Glos), with the
aid of a Combine fitted with headlights. By this method, the
harvest was completed shortly before mid-night, the wheat
remaining dry after a warm sunny day.

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN DAILIES
OF FRIDAY 9TH OCTOBER 1964

NORTH SEA GEOPHYSICAL OPERATIONS.
ERF.	G.	OCTOBER 1964
BRITISH PETROLEUM HAS BEEN AWARDED PRODUCTION
LICENCES BY THE MINISTER OF POWER, COVERING
SOME 2,200 SQUARE MILES IN AREA TO SEARCH FOR
AND PRODUCE OIL AND NATURAL GAS UNDER THE
NORTH SEA ADJACENT TO THE UNITED KINGDOM. THE
AREAS LIE OFF THE COAST OF DURHAM, YORKSHIRE
AND LINCOLNSHIRE.
			THE COMPANY HAS DRAWN UP PLANS FOR
ITS OWN SUBSTANTIAL DRILLING PROGRAMME. THE B.P.
AREA HAS BEEN DIVIDED INTO THREE PRODUCTION LICENCES, IN
EACH OF WHICH ONE DEEP TEST WILL INITIALLY BE
DRILLED: THE PROGRAMME FOR FURTHER TEST DRILLING
WILL BE ABOUT 12,000 FEET IN DEPTH AND WILL COST
AT LEAST £500,000. DRILLING OPERATIONS WILL
COMMENCE AS EARLY AS PRACTICABLE IN 1965.
GEOPHYSICAL WORK HAS ALREADY BEGUN IN ORDER
TO AID SELECTION OF DRILLING LOCATIONS.
PHOTO SHOWS:

A DEPTH CHARGE IS FIRED ABOUT 200 YARDS ASTERN
OF THE SURVEY VESSEL "TEXIN". THESE CHARGES
WHICH ARE PRIMED IN A SPECIAL CAGE, ATTACHED
TO THE FIRING LINE AND JETTISONED INTO WATER,
ARE FIRED AT THE RATE OF ALMOST ONE A MINUTE
DURING DAYLIGHT HOURS. THE EFFECT OF THE SHOCK
WAVES FROM THE DEPTH CHARGES ECHOED FROM THE
ROCK FORMATION BELOW THE SEA BED, ARE RELAYED
BY THE "STREAMER". SIGNALS FROM THE SHOCK WAVE
ARE FED INTO THE SHIP VIA THE "STREAMER" AND RECORDED
ON TAPE AS WELL AS BEING PHOTOGRAPHICALLY REPRODUCED
AS AN IMMEDIATE 	VISUAL CHECK.

G. 10055

SUN
PROPERTY
9 OCT 1964

"HIGH TIME" FOR HOP STRINGING.        MJH/rs.

In the hop fields of Kent, work is now in progress on the
annual task of "hop-stringing" - that is fixing up the
criss-cross strings from the top of the poles, along which
the growing hop-bines will be trained. To do this work,
then men have to perform a "circus act" - for the only way
then can rig up the strings and fix hooks to them, is by
walking on stilts.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:  42-years-old MR. GEORGE WELLS seen
"stil walking" in the Whitbread hop-field at Beltring, Paddock
Wood (Kent) where "stringing" is now in progress. Mr. Wells
has been doing this work every year for the past 20 years.
Beneath him pushing the barrow of twine is Mr. BERT BISHOP (54).

STUDENTS CLAIM URANIUM FIND IN CORNISH TIN MINE   D/P.1.

Six students, members of the Scientific and Geological
Society of Worksop College, Notts., claim to have found
a rich seam of uranium in the old Wheal Edward tin mine
near St. Just, Cornwall. The students are spending a
month's holidays volunteer workers for Mr. Paul Stein
of London who owns the rights of the mine. They have dug
out 18 cwts of rough ore, which they claim is 25% uranium
oxide. It has been sent to London for examination by the
Ministry of Supply.

PHOTO SHOWS: Mr. W. Billing, a skilled miner of St. Just,
is seen in centre examining the uranium in a piece of ore,
surrounded by some of the student miners.

activity: Buyers, wearing overalls to protect their clothes, examining white fox skins before bidding at the Hudson Bay sale

te.text:
BUYERS FROM REST OF WORLD FOR £1,000,000 WORTH OF FURS IN LONDON

There are now in London buyers from all parts of the world
attending the fur sales conducted by the London Fur Sales
Committee.  All through the winter valuable furs have been
collected by the distant posts in Northern Canada and have been
sent, mostly by slow and arduous travel, to London Most of
these posts are controlled by the Hudson Bay Company who own
most of the skins offered for sale in London.  About £1,000,000worth
are now at the Hudson Bay warehouse in Queen Victoria Street
and are being daily auctioned.

Photo shows:-  Buyers, wearing overalls to protect their clothes,
examining white fox skins before bidding at the Hudson Bay
sale today.
FOX Jany 26th.

activity: blacksmith ROBERT MARTIN seen at work outside his old stone forge at Ardigon, Killyleagh, showing horses and mending cart wheels

te.text:
AN EMERALD ISLE SMITHY.  MJH/M. 8.

A charming characteristic scene, fast disappearing from
the landscape of the British Isles in this mechanised age,
is the sight of the village smithy at work outside his
forge. However, in a few districts, particularly where
the contours of the land are hilly, making machines
impracticable, so that the horse is still a very necessary
part of farm life, there is still plenty of work for
the blacksmith. One such place is at Ardigon, Killyleagh,
Co. Down (N. Ireland), where the 'smith, 78-years-old
Robert Martin [strike-through] still gets enough of the work he loves
to keep him busy. Mr. Martin, a typical bit of "Ould 
Oirland" has been a blacksmith for 64 years.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: 78-years-old blacksmith ROBERT MARTIN,
seen at work outside his old stone forge at Ardigon, Killyleagh,
Co. Down, N. Ireland, where he can still find plenty of work,
showing horses, mending cart wheels etc.
FOX PHOTOS JUNE 16TH. 1955.

activity: The Queen waves to a 12-year-old Australian girl, Marilyn Deacon, outside the gates of Buckingham Palace.

te.text:
PROPERTY OF
[illegible] HERALD
21 NOV 1959
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

THE Queen waves to a little girl—and on both
their faces shines an I'm-so-glad-you-could-make-
it smile. Little Marilyn Deacon, the 12-year-old
Australian girl in London for a hole-in-the-heart
operation, wrote to the Queen saying how much
she wanted to see her. The Queen wrote back
telling her to be outside the gates of Buckingham
Palace yesterday. And everything went to plan.

COPYRIGHT
TO
PLANET NEWS LTD
(UNITED PRESS PHOTOS)
8, BOUVERIE STREET,
LONDON, E.C.4.

activity: Loading mail bags for dispatch to France at an Army Post Office in the home counties.

te.text:
TOMLIN. 			15.11.39.
THE ARMY POST OFFICE.
Somewhere in the home counties a staff
of some hundreds are daily handling thousands
of parcels and letters for our troops both
in England and Overseas.
Their greatest sorrow in life seems to be
that hundreds of letters and parcels each
day cannot be forwarded to our troops because
of incorrect addresses, and parcels packed in
such a way that the contents have to be re-
packed before being sent off, if the address is
readable.
O.P.S.
Loading mail bags for dispatch to France.

activity: Bus conductresses (clippies) demonstrating outside the Transport and General Workers' Union headquarters in Gower Street for equal rights, while a union official lectures their leader Kathleen Fincham.

te.text:
THE setting is the pavement
outside the London headquarters
of the Transport and General
Workers' Union in Gower Street.
Inside a meeting of busmen had
broken up after conductresses
marched in carrying banners
saying, 'We refuse to be
second-class workers.' The
women want to be allowed to drive
buses, and claim improved
pensions and sick pay. Rather
than discuss their grievances, the
men adjourned their meeting to
the scorn of the women who said,
'What are you afraid of?' This is
nothing but bigotry.' The words
must have smarted the busmen,
one of whom was George Fincham,
husband of the clippies' leader,
Kathy Fincham. Outside, Mr. and
Mrs. Fincham held a little meeting
of their own, and were joined by
another clippie, Doris Scott. Then
a union official arrived and gave
Mrs. Fincham a lecture on how not
to conduct union business. This
is the tableau in the picture, with
the official (in cap) lecturing Mrs.
Fincham, while her husband and
Doris Scott look on. Later Mrs.
Fincham went home to cook her
husband's dinner, at which the
debate continued.

JONES. SUN. 10.12.68.
Bus Conductresses Demonstrate at monthly conference T.G.W.U.
XXXXXX Women Clippies demonstrated outside the Headquarters of the T.G.W.U.
Gower St, nr Euston., before gate-crashing the conference with only men
in attendance. Immediately they entered the men decided to adjourn. Mrs
Kathleen Fincham, spokesman for the clippies who comes from Winchmore Hill,
had her husband George, a Union worker, driver in the meeting. After the
walk out by the men, Mrs Fincham was joined her husband George, seen bareheaded
on right, and another clippie Doris Scott on extreme right, xxxxx when
Mrs Fincham, seen holding bag, was called apart by a Union member and given
a talking to.
INDUS...MISC. WORKERS WOMEN EQUAL PAY ETC

activity: A general view of Mosley Common Colliery in Boothstown, Lancashire, showing a modern pithead as part of a reconstruction scheme.

te.text:
LANCASHIRE'S LARGEST COLLIERY
UNDER RECONSTRUCTION

The completion of half the coal
preparation plant, marks the end of the
first stage of the reconstruction scheme at
MOSLEY COMMON COLLIERY , BOOTHSTOWN, (Lancs.)
The largest colliery in Lancashire, Mosley
Common, employs more than 2,700 workers. When
the new scheme is complete coal from Sandhole
and Newtown collieries, in addition to that of
Mosley Common, will be wound electrically up
the one new shaft-now being completed.
Ultimately , 8,000 tons of coal each day will
be brought up this shaft from the three
collieries in two shifts. When finally complete
the MOSLEY COMMON coal preparation plant will
be the largest of its kind in Great Britain.
It is designed to treat a minimum of 600
tons of coal an hour, or working two shifts
8,000 tons per day- the whole of the coal as mined
with no hand selection whatever.
Large pieces of coal will be broken mechanically
to a maximum size of eight inches ( a provision
which domestic users will appreciate) and even the
very finest sizes of dust will be cleaned to a
low ash content. Washed slack or "smalls" will
be dried by a centrifugal machine at high speed
- thus enabling direct despatch from the pit
instead of having to stand insidings drying
for upwards of 24 hours. The total cost will be
more than half a million pounds.

PHOTO SHOWS:- A general view of MOSLEY COMMON
COLLIERY, BOOTHSTOWN, Lancashire , showing a modern
pithead

te.text:
A TYPICALLY ENGLISH CRAFT. PC/VAN.

One of the most typically English crafts
must surely be the making of cricket bats
and at Benjamin Warsop & Sons Limited, St.
John's Wood, London, near the famous Lord's
ground, fine bats have been produced for many
years. Some of the orders are bulk, for
large sports stores and export, but, some are
specially tailored to suit the requirements
of the top batsmen throughout the world.
Special orders are often produced under the
watchful eyes of 87 year-old, Mr.George Edward Hunt,
who started learning his craft at the age of
twenty-one - he is now the managing director
of the company but can nearly always be
found in one of the workshops supervising
the construction of the fine cricket bats.

Photo shows. DAVID MARKHAM, of Watford, Herts., a
young craftsman, seen fixing a handle to a new
cricket bat.

KEARNEY & TRECKER-C.V.A. LAUNCHES FIRST
BRITISH-BUILT MILWAUKEE-MATIC
---------------------------------------

The first British-built Milwaukee-Matic machining centre
has been introduced by Kearney & Trecker-C.V.A. Ltd.,
the south coast machine tool enterprise. It is the
Series Ea model which will carry out the individual
operations of milling, drilling, boring, reaming and
tapping from one point without the need to transfer the
workpiece to another machine. The entire operation is
carried out by punched tape control from a computer and
provides dramatic savings in production and setup time
compared to conventional methods. A feature of the Ea
is its ability to meet any machining requirement from
the average small batch manufacture to long run product-
ion. With the Ea model tool changes are made auto-
matically in five seconds from a drum-type tool magazine
which holds 15 tools.

activity: Hostess Elizabeth Sterland with Swedish businessman Alv Gregersen at the Royal Garden Hotel in London.

te.text:
TWO ATTRACTIVE girls,
eager to be of assistance,
waited at London Airport
yesterday to welcome
visitors from all over
Europe attending a con-
ference here.
But they waited in vain.
For their stall was so well
concealed that only one
delegate out of 950 man-
aged to find it.
And last night the firm
which organised the con-
ference of Pulp and Paper
Industrial Technology did
not trouble to conceal
their anger.
Mrs. Fay Pannell, who
introduced the hostess
service for delegates, said:
"London Airport have not
been at all helpful. They
are, in fact, very difficult
to get on with.
'Useless'
"If the airport already
had an efficient reception
system, other people would
not be needed to do it."
Mrs. Pannell's com-
plaint: "We felt the girls
should be in a good posi-
tion in the airport lounge.
But we have been given
a small stall right at the
end of the main concourse

-and charged £55 rent
for three days.
"It is useless - just
money down the drain."
Still, there was no lack
of attention for the dele-
gates last night at the
Royal Garden Hotel, head-
quarters of the con-
ference.
Fifteen hostesses - each
paid £3 a day - were on
duty in their couturier-
designed uniforms. All in-
tent on maintaining what
Mrs. Pannell called "a
strictly business relation-
ship with the delegates."

te.text:
£8 MILLION OIL REFINERY PLANNED FOR BELFAST
26  10.11.60.
AN ARTIST'S IMPRESSION OF HOW THE £8 MILLION OIL REFINERY
PLANNED FOR BELFAST WILL LOOK WHEN COMPLETED. THE SITE IS
ON RECLAIMED LAND TO THE NORTH-EAST OF THE EXISTING OIL
STORAGE INSTALLATIONS IN THE MUSGRAVE CHANNEL OF BELFAST
HARBOUR, AND IN THE TOP LEFT THE SHIPYARDS OF HARLAND AND
WOLF CAN BE SEEN. THE REFINERY, WHICH IS TO BE BUILT FOR
THE BRITISH PETROLEUM COMPANY LTD., WILL HAVE AN INITIAL
CAPACITY FOR HANDLING 1,300,000 TONS OF CRUDE OIL ANNUALLY,
AND THE REFINED PRODUCTS WILL BE MARKETED IN NORTHERN IRELAND
AND SOME EXPORT MARKETS. WORK IS EXPECTED TO BEGIN SOMETIME
NEXT YEAR AND THE REFINERY, THE FIRST IN NORTHERN IRELAND,
SHOULD TAKE ABOUT TWO YEARS TO COMPLETE.

COPYRIGHT PHOTO ISSUED BY
CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
6 & 7, GOUGH SQUARE,
FLEET STREET, LONDON, E.C.4.
FLEET STREET 2266/7.

te.text:
NORTHANTS.
BRITAIN LAYS ITS FIRST TELEVISION CABLE.

Post Office enginers have begun to lay the first longe
distance television cable in Britain. The cable will stretch
from London to Birmingham. There is only one wire in the
cable. The wire will be able to carry 20 voices
simultaneously , will relay sound, broadcast and television
programmes . As it is hoped that a regular B.B.C. public
television service will begin next June it is possible
that the B.B.C. may televise the Coronation ceremony.

Photo shows- Laying miles of television cable at
Northampton to-day, the first television cable in Britain.
Fox Feb 20th. 36.

te.text:
PRINCESS ELIZABETH REPRESENTS THE KING AT TROOPING  7-6-51
THE COLOUR

H.M. the King was represented by Princess Elizabeth 
at today's King Birthday Trooping the Colours Parade
at the Horse Guards Parade.  The Princess, riding her
chestnut, Winston, wore the scarlet tunic of colonel 
of the Grenadier Guards with a dark blue riding skirt.
Her tricorne hat with white plume fixed into a grenade
on the left side is an exact copy of that of a colonel 
of the Regiment of 1745. 

INP PHOTO SHOWS: Princess Elizabeth photographed at the 
saluting base as the Guards march past 
in front of Buckingham Palace. On the 
balcony watching can be seen, the Queen, 
Queen Mary, Prince Charles, Princess 
Margaret and King Haakon and Princess 
Astrid of Norway. 

PICTURE BY E. WING

te.text: File INDUS Aviation Post War - Air Liners Brit - Bristol "Brabazon"

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY, Oct 21st.
ENGLISH VILLAGE MAKES WAY FOR GIANT PLANE
20.10.46.
Sacrificed to the cause of progress, the village of CHARLTON,
near Bristol, England, has been demolished to make room for
a runway spacious enough to allow the first take-off of the
giant Bristol "Brabazon" air liner prototype now under con-
struction at the famous works. A vast assembly hall is
also being built because she cannot be put together in any
existing building.
Features of the great aircraft are - wing span 230ft, height
50ft at rudder, and length 177ft. All-up weight 125 tons,
and sleeping berths for 80 passengers for night travel. It is
designed to fly direct between London and New York or
Montreal, and gas turbines in the wings accessible during
flight will give her a speed of 350 mph at 35,000 ft and her
range will be 5,000 miles. The picture shows workmen fixing
centre section wing ribs with the giant fuselage taking shape
in the background. The man in the wing illustrates how it
is possible to attend to the power units, which are built into
the wing, in flight.

 UNDAMAGED.

TO APPEAR ON TELEVISION.      MJH/HT.

The Chelsea Pottery, formed 15 months ago by David
Rawnsley, a former film art director, is already
becoming famous. The Victoria and Albert Museum
recently acquired three bowls and a dish produced
at the pottery, since the museum authorities consider
the glazing technique unique and now Mrs. Rawnsley
wife of the founder of the pottery, is to give a talk
and demonstration on clay modelling on television in
the near future. Besides being a commercial venture, the

Mr. Rawnsley in Montparnasse, Paris), providing facilities
for it's members, which include, actresses, dentists, office
workers and professional potters, to use potters' wheels
and kilns to produce their own work.

a talk and demonstration on clay modelling on television,

activity: the bathroom of a dilapidated house under investigation for the Rachman housing scandal

te.text:
PETER RACHMAN is dead, but fear
still haunts St. Stephen's Gardens
and Chepstow Road, Paddington—heart
of the empire where once he squeezed
rents from crumbling bricks.
Landlords, some of them linked with Rachman,
are selling properties as fast as they can. New
landlords are taking over with the aim of making
a fast profit. They want the tenants out, either
to resell at a profit or
else to pack in more
people paying more
money.
And so the rent bullies
still bluster at the door in
Rachman's streets.
Mrs. Annie O'Keefe has
found that a change of land-
lord does not necessarily
mean an improvement on
the Rachman regime.
She has a single top-floor room
at 11, St. Stephen's Gardens.
Her tenancy is protected under
the Rent Act.
But in May the property
changed hands and Mrs. O'Keefe
now pays her rent to the Dis-
tinctive Property Company, who
have an address at 110, Shore-
ditch High Street, London.
STRUCK HER
Since they took over Mrs.
O'Keefe has been subjected to
continual threats, designed, she
believes, to make her quit the
property.
Twice she has been called on
by a man called Richards and
another named De Freitas (a
former associate of Rahman).
They claimed to be acting for
the landlord.
Richards and de Freitas
demanded the rent — which
was not due for several days.
Mrs. O'Keefe keeps the door
of her room chained. On the
second visit, however, the two
men forced the door. In doing
so they bruised Mrs. O'Keefe's
knee. She has also told her
solicitor that one of them struck
her on the arm.
The pair went away when
Mrs. O'Keefe threatened to get
the police. And since she put
the matter in the hands of a
solicitor she has not been visited
again.

DAILY HERALD
Copyright
Photograph
BY L. BLANDFORD
NUMBER..................

This is the bathroom at 13, St. Stephen's Gardens, one of
the houses visited by the Herald investigating team

BLANDFORD.D.H. 18.7.63. Story R. Adams.
RACHMAN STORY.
O.P.S. The Bathroom in No. 13 St. Stephens Gardens, Paddington.

activity: Operating a digging machine in the construction of the London Airport traffic tunnel.

te.text:
LONDON AIRPORT TRAFFIC TUNNEL GROWS  D/FM

Considerable progress has been made during the
summer months on the 4-way vehicular traffic
tunnel which will link London Airport terminal
area with the ondon-Bath road. When completed
this tunnel will be the only means of communi-
cation between the airport and the surrounding
land area and will be approached by two long
ramps leading from the Bath road, one of which is
almost surfaced. The central area will house all
the passenger and administrative buildings, which
are at present strung out along the northern
perimeter of the Airport, and will be dominated
by a lofty Control Tower. The 2,600 ft. long
tunnel comprises two single-way traffic roadways
flanked on either side by two single-way passenger
and cycle ways.

PHOTO SHOWS: Operating a digging machine in the
construction of the London Airport traffic
tunnel.

COAL BOARD HAS ITS OWN UNIFORM.

With the handing over of the mines
to public ownership, a new uniform
has appeared at Lansdowne House,
Berkeley Square, W., temporary
headquarters of the National Coal Board.
The uniform, which resembles a
police inspector's, is dark blue with
patch pockets and chromium buttons.
The initials 'NCB' are on the lapels.
Members of the staff who have to wear
the uniform are still uncertain about
whether they will have to give up
clothing coupons for it.

chief porter at Lansdowne House, wearing
the new uniform. 'I like it', he says,
'but the coupons...?'
CHI January 1st 1947 PN.r.

activity: building construction using hot concrete to allow work to continue in freezing temperatures at a site in Houndsditch, London

te.text: Industry.. Building and Construction.. Misc... Anti bad weather measures

HOT CONCRETE BEATS THE WINTER

Britain's building industry can now beat
frost and snow - with hot concrete. Work
goes on at this large building site in
Houndsditch, London, even when the temperature
drops well below zero. Tons of aggregate and
hundreds of gallons of water are heated by
Calor propane before being fed into the mixer.
As a result, the concrete sets before frost
can attack it. The process was developed by
the Calor Gas company earlier this year.

Contractors at the Houndsditch site are
Myton Ltd., who are erecting an eight-floor
block of offices and shops, and a 14-storey
car park for City and Southern Properties Ltd.
Architects for the project are R. Seifert and
Partners; consulting engineers, C. J. Pell and
Partners; quantity surveyors, John Reddick
and Partners.

Further enquiries: David Harrison,
Frank O'Shanohun Associates
Ltd.,
34 Bouverie Street,
London, E.C.4.

FLEet Street 9891

NO REPRODUCTION FEE.

activity: MR. H.W. DAY selecting stones and MR. M. DAY cutting roofing tiles during the restoration of a Cotswold stone cottage at Winson.

te.text:
NEW LEASE OF LIFE FOR OLD COTTAGE.     MJH/MAE.
An old Cotswold stone cottage at Winson in the Coln
Valley (Glos), belonging to Col. R. Henriques, is now
in the process of repair and modernisation, one of many
such restoration schemes which are now taking place in
the Cotswolds. Many of the picturesque Cotswold villages
are being greatly improved by such work, undertaken on the
incentive given by the Slum Clearance Act and Council
Grants to owners to repair old cottages in their original
style, but with all modern interior conveniences.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: MR. H.W. DAY (left) a local builder
whose family have specialised in Cotswold stone work and
roofing for generations seen selecting stones for the
work on the cottage at Winson (Glos). He has restored nearly
20 such cottages in the Coln Valley. With him (right) MR.
M. DAY, stone roof tiler, is seen cutting roofing tiles.

activity: 70 year old blacksmith Nathaniel Barber working at his forge at Milford Mill near Salisbury.

te.text:
Bell.                  DH                  1.2.44.
NAT'S SCORE IS 25,000 not out.
In the tiny hamlet of Milford situated on the
outskirts of Salisbury lives 70 year old Nathaniel
Barber, Blacksmith for 53 years. Nat belongs to
a fast dying profession, for blacksmiths are now
becoming a rarity.
Motor Engineer is the new term for where Nat used
to shoe over 200 horses six times a year, now only
20 come to him to be reshod.
Nat's father was a blacksmith as were four of his
eight brothers of whom he is the only one left.
In spite of the lack of horses to shoe, Nat
persuaded his 40 year old son to learn the craft
and now when Nat passes on, Ronald will become the
fourth generation of Barber - Blacksmith.
Nat boasts of the time he shoed famous racehorses
in the district.
Nat estimates that he has made and forged 25,000
shoes in his 53 years and hopes to make a few more
thousand yet. He works from dawn till dusk six
days a week throughout the year.
There is another son, Horace, profession motor
engineer.
O.P.S.1    70 year old Nat. Barber at the forge
           at Milford Mill.

activity: demonstration of a portable vaporising machine using pyrethrum insecticide to kill mosquitoes at Imperial Airways laboratories in Battersea

te.text:
SAYERS.        1983-5236/90001        18.10.38.

THEY WERE IN A "DEVILISH MOOD".
Imperial Airways overcome menace of mosquitoes
in tropical countries.

Imperial Airways invited a number of Pressmen
to their laboratories in Battersea, to see a
device similar to that now employed by many
London Hospitals for disinfecting their wards.
It consists of a portable vaporising machine
which permeates the atmosphere with a pyrethrum
insecticide which kills the mosquitoes which are
liable to carry disease within a few minutes.
O.P.S.
25 mosquitoes in each of these little cages
were nice and warm in front of a gas fire,
so that they would be right on form and in
fine fettle for the demonstration.  It is
needless to say none of them survived the test.

activity: The prepackaging installation at Charringtons depot at Radley where solid fuel is packed into multiwall paper sacks and palletised for storage.

te.text: Ind - Fuel - Coal Depots nd Dumps inc. Sale of

Prepacked solid fuel is being sold in Oxford from this week by Charrington
Gardner Locket delivered in 56 lb. and 28 lb. paper sacks. Known as
Pak-o-Fuel, the delivery service is so clean an operation that the prepacked
fuel is brought to the consumer by coalmen dressed in white overalls.
Picture shows:  The prepackaging installation at Charringtons depot at
Radley, near Oxford, where a wide range of solid fuel is packed into
56 lb. and 28 lb. multiwall paper sacks at high speed.
By using the latest method of palletisation, sufficient quantities of the
prepacked fuel are being stored to meet peak demands.  The empty pallets
(left foreground) are fed one by one onto a platform which is then raised
hydraulically to the level of the sack conveyor.
The operator has only to guide the sack into position on the pallet
without having to completely lift them.  The operator can rotate the
platform to load the pallet and lower it sufficiently to load the next
layer of sacks.
When the pallet is fully loaded it is lowered and moved sideways on to
the rails (right foreground), where it is removed by fork lift truck,
and the same movement pushes the next empty pallet into position on the
platform.

Issued on behalf of:
Reed Medway Sacks Limited,
Larkfield,
Kent.

Enquiries: Allen Loates
Reed House,
82 Piccadilly,
London. W.1.
GROsvenor 4020

te.text:
ONE OF ENGLAND'S DYING CRAFTS.   MJH/MAE.

One of the many attractions to visitors to this country
are the thatched roofs of cottages and barns, which are
typical of England. Slowly such roofs are disappearing
and being replaced by others, since roof thatching is
a dying craft. There is, however, still plenty of work
for the decreasing number of skilled roof thatchers as
many of these roofs are being preserved in their original
state.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: Mr. George Pocketts, one of the decreasing
number of skilled roof thatchers in this country, at work
on a barn belonging to Mr. J. Denley, at Woodmancote (Glos).
The previous thatch on this barn has lasted about 40 years.

The copy from the author goes to Linotype
machines - they have a keyboard similar to
that of a typewriter - which transforms the
printed word into metal type.  The type is
made up into a page form which has a
facsimile taken off it in paper flong,
from which the metal cast is produced.
Plates are assembled in special order on the
bed of the printing machine and after the
application of ink, the printed sheet is
produced.
The printed sheet goes through nearly half-
a dozen operations such as folding, gathering,
sewing and cutting, when it is transformed
into the bound copy sold to the public.
Real leather is used for the making of cases.

activity: Joey, a pit pony, coming up from Carl Colliery in Ashington for the last time upon his retirement.

te.text:
HAVE you ever wondered
what happens to pit
ponies when their life's
work underground is
done?
Last week, after seeing this
picture — it shows Joey,
the pony, coming up from
Carl Colliery, Ashington,
for the last time — I set
out to find the answer.
It shocked me. I was told that
1,000 pit ponies are "retired"
by the Coal Board every year,
and 700 of them are destroyed.
Simply because there are not
enough suitable homes for
them. Rather than condemn
ponies used to the comrade-
ship of the miners under-
ground to lonely lives in
empty fields, they are pain-
lessly put to sleep.
One man is trying desperately
hard to find a better way out.
Chief Inspector Bill Burr, of
the R.S.P.C.A. at Scarborough,
spends all his spare time find-
ing homes for retired pit
ponies.
Last year alone he rescued 50

ponies. He does it as much
for the miners as for the
ponies. "I've seen many a
miner cry when his pony has
gone up the shaft for the last
time," says Bill Burr.
But he agrees with the Coal
Board that empty fields are
no places for retired ponies.
They can only go to those who
have proper stabling.
No pony must be used com-
mercially for pleasure rides—
and horse dealers are strictly
barred.
"They work underground for at
least 10 years. They are
much loved by the men so
they deserve proper care in
their retirement," says the
Coal Board with an unex-
pected warmth of feeling.
Chief Inspector Burr should
get more help for his work of
mercy. Over 7,000 ponies toil
to give us coal. It's dear
enough, I agree. But not all
that dear, surely?
Industry - Fuel & Power - Coal - Pits - Ponies.

Under Carl
from Ashwell
heaven's a home.

BUILDING COLLAPSES ON WORKMEN NEAR LYCEUM.  Story P. Moorhead.
O.P.S.
Workmen and Firemen work frantically to release the

THEY were pulling down a house in
Exeter Street, just off the Strand.
The usual rough hearty banter, the
usual soloist singing a pop tune, and all
the loud thud and crackle that goes with
demolition work.
Then it happened. Tons of brick and
plaster roared down.
SWEAT
And underneath is one of their mates.
With bare hands they sweat into the
job of freeing him, grabbing through the
dust and debris at the bricks and rafters.
Firemen arrive. Together they go on
heaving away the rubble, through
precious minute after precious minute.
Bleeding fingers torn on masonry are
ignored. So is the threatening danger
of another fall of overhanging brickwork.
Forty-five minutes are gone.
TEARS
A hand is spotted . . A workmate
shouts: "I've found him."
Ambulancemen move in. Workmates
and firemen on their knees scoop away
the dirt and wood and debris from the
buried man.
Shoulders droop. Men take off their
caps . .
They have lost their race against time.
Their mate is dead.

224476  LUD

London: Glittering, golden sovereigns, a small

back there.

te.text:
V. 23046.

STEPNEY-POPLAR RECONSTRUCTION AREA.

    The London County Council will consider on Tuesday
next, 5th., February, initial proposals for the
long-term redevelopment of an extensive area of
1,960 acres in Stepney and Poplar.
    This photograph shows a model indicating the lines
of the proposed redevelopment by the Council of an
area of 33 1/2 acres at Ocean Street, Stepney (part
of the Stepney-Poplar Reconstruction Area), as a
new housing site. (See also photograph No. V. 23246).
    The development scheme provides for mixed types
of accommodation consisting of two-storey terrace
houses with gardens, and three-storey, four storey
and eight-storey blocks of flats. The total
accommodation will be 1,145 dwellings and in
addition 12 shops, 3 children's fitted playgrounds
and about 90 perambulator sheds will be provided.
Lifts will be provided in the eight-storey blocks of
flats and provision will be made for a nursery group
of from 30 to 40 children in one of the blocks
of dwellings, with a small playing space adjoining.
February 1946.

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION TUESDAY'S EVENINGS, Jan 21st.
"QUEEN ELIZABETH" OF THE AIR TAKES SHAPE
21.1.47.
In the early summer it is hoped that the Bristol "Brabazon"
prototype of Britain's largest airplane, will make her first
flight.
Work on the giant aircraft began just over a year ago, and
her construction will have involved an outlay of £4,000,000
the destruction of a village and a golf course, and the
building of a special runway costing £2,000,000.
She will be 177ft long with a wing span of 230ft (30ft longer
than the distance between the main structures of Tower
Bridge), and weight 130 tons, and eight Centaurus gas-turbines
of 2500 hp each will power her. "Brabazon's" later models
will carry 100 passengers in comfort at 250 mph on British
Atlantic services. In this picture two men are working high
up on one of the platforms built among the scaffolding which
surrounds the massive fuselage which nestled in a steel
cradle.

THIS IS THE PROPERTY OF THE

AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

BRITISH OFFICIAL PHOTOGRAPH No. P 446
(Issued by the Ministry of Information - Crown
Copyright Reserved).

3,610 men and women employed in a famous North country
iron and steel works signed a resolution "that our
maximum endeavours will be devoted to sustain
the national war effort - and as a token of our
intention we will forego Christmas holidays so that
normal production can continue".
Johnny Thompson, who signed the resolution on behalf of
his mates "slagging" one of the furnaces in
the steel Rolling Mills.

BRITISH OFFICIAL PHOTOGRAPH No.
ISSUED BY
PHOTOGRAPHIC NEWS AGENCIES, LTD,
30, FLEET STREET, E.C.4.
TEL: CENTRAL 2260

NO FREEZE-UP AT JACKBLOCK

In the Arctic weather which has hampered work on building sites,
normal working has continued on Costain's Jackblock site in
Coventry. No men have been laid off, there has been no short

schedule. This has been achieved by surrounding the three lower
floors with a large plastic tent and installing blower heaters,
thus bringing factory conditions to a building site.

other work continues.

activity: Nissen hut wives and their children carrying water from the camp cookhouse to their huts on the Peterborough site

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN SUNDAY NEWSPAPERS, AUGUST 11th.

EX SERVICEMEN'S FAMILIES MOVE INTO EMPTY ARMY HUTS -
WAR OFFICE DECIDE TO TAKE NO ACTION.

Unable to find homes elsewhere because of the housing shortage,
ex Servicemen and their wives and children have moved into
unoccupied military huts in St. Paul's Road, Peterborough,
Northamptonshire. Although some notices to quit were served
on Peterborough squatters, it is reported that the War Office
and the Ministry of Health have decided to take no action
against the people who have taken possession of unoccupied
Army camps in many parts of the country.
Among the families installed on the Peterborough site are
Mr. and Mrs. Harry Joseph Vines and their 3 1/2-year-old daughter
Patricia. Mr. Vines, now an inspector in a Diesel factory,
is a former Petty Officer in the Navy who won the British Empire
Medal for bringing a lifeboat safely to land after it had been
39 days in the Atlantic following the torpedoing of a troopship.
Whilst recovering from his ordeal in New York he met Caroline -
now his wife - who comes from Brooklyn.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Nissen hut wives and their children carrying water
from the camp cookhouse to their huts on the Peterborough site.
Left to right - Mrs. Helen Holmes and daughter Margaret, aged 6;
Patricia Vines, aged 3 1/2, and Mrs. Caroline Vines.
LUD August 10th 1946 PN.r.

COPYRIGHT
PLANET NEWS LTD.
3 JOHNSON'S COURT,
FLEET STREET, E.C.4.
PHONE: CENTRAL 3671/3.

te.text:
AN OIL REFINERY IN ENGLAND GOES INTO ACTION
29.6.51.
While the news of the Persian oil dispute still fills the
headlines, the second distillation unit in the large ex-
tensions to the great STANLOW (Cheshire) Refinery has now
been completed ahead of schedule, and is working. It treble
the refinery's output to over 3 million tons a year, and is
only part of the extensions in progress. Five further plant
including a catcracker, are yet to come into operation, and
on completion in January 1952, Stanlow will produce a com-
plete range of petroleum products from high quality petrol
the heavy fuel oil.
This picture shows a huge welded steel absorber column,
weighing 240 tons and over 170 feet long and nearly 10 feet
in diameter being erected at Stanlow refinery. Highly
specialised equipment was employed in raising this enormous
structure which was manufactured by Babcock and Wilcox at
their RENFREW works. In the back ground is the refinery's
concrete water cooling tower, largest of its kind in the
world.

activity: Building a 50-ft fishing and pleasure boat inside a barn.

te.text:
50-FT. BOAT BEING BUILT IN A BARN.              AW/HT.

The largest boat ever to be built in the area is under
construction on a farm at Pevensey, Sussex.  She will
be the Eastbourne Queen, a fishing and pleasure boat,
and she is being built by Mr. R. Pragnell, of Westham.
Mr. Pragnell has had several problems to overcome -
for instance, the barn was'nt big enough to take the
boat's keel, so one end had to be knocked down and an
extension built.  And when the boat is finished, about
next May, he will have to knock down the walls of the
barn to get her out.  It will then be towed out and
transported across the fields to the water.

Photo shows-          Building the 50-ft boat in the barn
at Pevensey.  The vessel will be 13ft broad, and will
be the biggest on Eastbourne Beach.
Fox Feb 23. 49.                398848

te.text: Industry.. Building and Construction.. Anti weather

DOMED PLASTIC HOME FOR TRADITIONAL MARKET
December 10th 1968 PAP 137154-1  (A-0)

DOMED PLASTIC HOME FOR TRADITIONAL MARKET

To make room for an overpass on the A 13 in
Essex, 150 traders from Basildon's Pitsea
market are to be rehoused in four huge
Abstracta plastic clad domes, the first
time these have been used as semi-permanent
buildings in this country.
The domes construction is the brain-child
of Danish designer, Poel Cadovius.
One of the market domes, has been half-
sprayed with concrete, nine feet upwards
from its base.
The domes are expected to remain on the new
market site between eight to ten years, and
if successful may become a permanency.
The advantage to the traders, is that
in their traditional market which was largely
in the open-air, the new venture will offer
them complete cover from the unreliable
English weather.
December 10th 1968 PAP 137154-1  (A-0)
PRESS ASSOCIATION PHOTOS
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN EVENING PAPERS OF
TUESDAY DECEMBER 10th 1968

activity: Alan Doyle and Anthony Woodcock loading old film reels into a furnace at the John Betts bullion firm to extract silver.

te.text:
Yesterday thousands of feet of old
film—some showing multi-million-
pound epics of the silver screen
—went up in a puff of smoke to
produce real silver for Britain.
Silver is in short supply and
expensive, at 12s. 3d. an ounce.
Which is why cast-off film from
the cinema, and T.V is sent
every day to the 200-year-old
bullion firm of John Betts.
'There the reels are burnt in a
furnace to extract their silver
content.
Yesterday it was the turn of
'Camelot,' 'The Informer' and
dozens of petrol and soap powder
advertisements to be loaded into the
furnace by Alan Doyle and Anthony
Woodcock.
On other days it could
be old 'Bootsie And
Snudge' films from T.V—
or even "blue" films.
The result each week is
30 1,000oz. ingots of silver
worth £18,000.
Director Christopher
Betts said: "We get
everything from epics
down to the mistakes
which famous actors make
and never want shown.
Security
"We have tight security
to ensure that everything
is burned and no film is
kept back for private view-
ing."
But he added: "We
recently managed to save
a David Attenborough
series which had not been
shown. The BBC cleared
it out by mistake. But one
of their men was here for
hours and managed to
save most of it.
"We reckon the aver-
age small photographer
could save £50 a year in
silver which he usually
pours down the drain or
throws away.
"One man we know now
has solid silver paper
weights from his waste so
that he can up-stage his
rivals."

The
silver
screen
gives
up
its
silver

te.text:
PICTURE FROM THE AIR -- 111 MEN ENTOMBED IN PIT DISASTER AT
WHITEHAVEN, CUMBERLAND.

Five rescue parties fought their way through the under sea
workings of the "William Pit, Whitehaven, Cumberland, in a
search for 111 men trapped by an explosion.
Nine doctors, and ambulances summoned from as far away as
Carlisle-40 miles distant- waited at the pithead, among
shawled and weeping women.
One hundred and twenty men were in the pit when the explosion
took place. Ten of them are known to be safe, and seven of
that number remained below with the rescue parties.
PHOTO SHOWS:-- An air view of the scene of the disaster at
the William Pit, Whitehaven Cumberland. Lines of ambulances
are waiting as rescue workers and anxious relatives and friends
wait for the latest news of the rescue efforts.
And August 16th 1947 PH

[Seal of the Association of British Chambers of Commerce: INDUSTRY COMMERCE TRANSPORT]

that the Queen is the Association's patron.

PRESS INFORMATION
Issued by
ESSO PETROLEUM COMPANY, LIMITED
36 QUEEN ANNE'S GATE, LONDON, S.W.I
TELEPHONE: WHITEHALL 5151
(Esso logo)
DATE 27th July, 1956 For Release Immediate Ref. No. 882
For additional information please refer to R. B. Sawrey-Cookson Extension 20
or after 7 p.m. telephone: WEStern 6145
OIL AND AUTOMATION
Automation has long been a feature of oil refining operations.
This photograph shows part of the control panel of the new £4 million
Fluid Catalytic Hydroformer at the Esso Refinery, Fawley, which processes
raw petrol obtained by primary distillation, and converts it into a very
high quality petrol.
Miniature instruments to record and control flow, pressure,
temperature, levels and so on, are let into the panel at positions
corresponding to those at which they operate on the plant.
The temperature console (foreground) indicates on the dials
some 200 temperature points in the plant.
The Hydroformer, capable of processing from 350,000 to
525,000 gallons a day, is operated by six men per shift. Of this
number, only one is present at all times, others only coming in
periodically to log operating conditions, as shown here.

activity: Introduction of a young gorilla named Meng to a baby chimpanzee named Jacqueline at London Zoo

te.text:
A NEW HUSBAND FOR "MOINA"

The Belgian Government have presented the London Zoo
with a new husband for "Moina".  He isn't old enough
or big enough to go in with her yet, as he is only
about a year old.  "Meng", as he is called after
the village where he was found, is a sturdy and
intelligent little youngster of the Mountain mf or
Kivu race of Gorilla.  When he grows up he will be
almost twice the size of the late lamented "Mok".
Male Kivu Gorillas, when fully grown, weigh up to
600 pounds.  "Meng" is being introduced to-day to
Jacqueline", the baby Chimpanzee at the Zoo which
has been brought up on the bottle by her keepers.  It
is hoped that they will take to each other and be
company for each other until "Meng" is big enough
to put up with "Moina".

activity: an inspector examining the moulded envelope of a rubber hot water bottle during the return to peace-time production

te.text:
LONG LAST - THE RETURN OF THE RUBBER HOT WATER BOTTLE.

The big switch-over to peace-time production in the large war
factories, is now in full swing. Rubber, that vital necessity
in the manufacture of the munitions of war, has now been re-
leased for the production of a greatly needed article - the
Hot Water Bottle. Our series of pictures secured at a factory
in Streatham, shews the reversion to peace-time schedule where
a few months ago, the workers were busy on the products of war-
dinghies, anti-aircraft fuze covers, and a thousand and one
other things. Thousands of hot water bottles, are being turned
out each week, but about 25% are for export, and on the home
market, priority is given to sick people, expectant mothers etc.
At present the 'mixture' is half natural rubber and half
synthetic, and this limits the colour range. Most people prefer
red from the present selection, and many manufacturers produce
this colour only, but we are looking forward to the days when
all natural rubber can be used, and the pre-war range of colours
can return.

Photograph shows :- An inspector examining the moulded
envelope.
FOX PHOTOS JAN 15th 46. 333489.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

activity: conveyors and external facilities of the coke-oven and by-product plant at Nantgarw

te.text:
STEPHENS OF CARDIFF.  D.H.  20-6-51.
THE COKE-OVEN AND BY-PRODUCT PLANT AT NANTGARW.
The Nantgarw plant, designed to be both functional and pleasing to the eye, is laid out amongst plants ans trees. The coke-ovens are to be fired next month and preparations are well in hand.
OPS.  The gleaming white maze of conveyors, with its brightly painted windows, will transport 1,500 tons of coal per day from the railway sidings to the ovens.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
REC: 21 JUN 1951
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

HERE are some of the
cased-in conveyers which
will feed 1,500 tons of blended
coking coal a day to the Coal
Board's 48 new ovens at
Nantgarw, Glamorgan.

The ovens and by-products
plant, built at a cost of
£2,500,000, will be run by 140
men.

They will have a daily output
of 18,000,000 cubic feet of gas,
1,100 tons of coke, 3,000 gallons
of benzol, 16 tons of ammonia
liquid and 40 tons of tar.

Entrance to the plant is
flanked by flower beds, and tree-
lined roads run through it. Next
door is the reconstructed Nant-
garw Colliery which, in two
years, will supply the plant with
two-thirds of its coal needs.

And nearby is Treforest Trad-
ing Estate, with its neat rows
of factories.

The plant was to have been
opened by the King on July 17.
But although he has had to
cancel his Welsh visit, the ovens
will be fired on schedule. As
they heat up, there will be eight
weeks final preparation for pro-
duction.

te.text:
XHN)           BORING TWO MILES FOR OIL

Hundreds of men are now hard at work on the slopes of
Portsdown Hill, near Portsmouth, preparing for the
gigantic task of penetrating twice as far beneath the
surface of England as ever before. In this peaceful
spot engineers are making ready to drill to a point
10,000 feet - or nearly two miles - under the ground
in a search for oil. The hole is to be drilled with the
most modern of machinery, the work being carried out
under the supervision of expert mining engineers who
have been brought from the oilfields of Persia. Ports-
down Hill was decided on as the site for boring after a
careful survey by geologists.

Photo shows:- Workmen hoisting staircasing up the 136ft.
derrick which has been erected at Portsdown.

EVICTED FAMILY CAMP ON PAVEMENT.

FURNITURE ON THE PAVEMENT, WHERE THEY HAVE CAMPED FOR

MR. BERNARD CLARK, 29, A £9 13s 6d A WEEK PAINTER AND HIS
FAMILY WERE EVICTED BY THE FINCHLEY COUNCIL FROM THEIR HOME
UNDER A COMPULSORY PURCHASE ORDER, AND NOW THE FAMILY CAMP

AND SON INTO A HOSTEL, BUT THEY HAVE REFUSED, THE COUNCIL
ALSO OFFERED TO RE-HOUSE THEM WITH MRS. CLARK'S PARENTS IN

DIDN'T WANT TO LEAVE.

11TH OCTOBER, 1957 PILS

te.text:
INLAND TELEPHOTO   YEP   LONDON BUREAU
IN 416049
"MINER SAFE" :
WOMBWELL, Yorks : Mr MORGAN CLAYTON is carried on a
stretcher by his workmates here today. Four miners, trapped
for nine and a half hours at a gas-filled coal face at
Cortonwood Colliery, died before rescue workers reached
them just before dawn today. The miners were overcome by
deadly methane gas which got into the underground workings
after the roof subsided.
At first it was hoped that the men
would be found alive but unconscious. But after rescue
workers got to them a doctor went from the pit bottom to the
seam and found them dead.
Mr Clayton was the second man to
be got out alive today.
20th June, 1961 - pn-on

te.text:
GOSPORT BUILDS MILLIONAIRE'S YACHT - FOR DOLLARS    D/ VIG

Some 60 men are at present engaged in building the largest
yacht to be made in Britain since the war, at Gosport. It
is a composite 125-ton ketch, with a 70-foot waterline,
ordered by 45-year-old American tobacco millionaire, Mr.
Richard J. Reynolds. The craft is built mainly of teak on
steel frames, with stern timbers of Mahogany. It is expected
to be ready for launching by June, will cost about £60,000
which Mr. Reynolds will pay in dollars.

deck on the forehead of the new yacht, the 785 as it is

te.text:
WORLD'S FIRST CATAMARAN DRILLING VESSEL DEVELOPED.

Latest addition to a series of unique international
floating drilling rigs is an unusual 278 ft. twin hulled
catamaran. Called the E.W. THORNTON the vessel is capable
of boring more than 4 miles beneath the ocean bed when in
600 ft. of water.
Shape and size of the 6,000 ton craft is said to make
it an "engineering marvel" in the field of floating oil
drilling rigs. Built to withstand rough seas, it is held
in place by eight 10-ton anchors to prevent drifting.
Christened at ORANGE, (Texas), the Thorton travels
under its own power at speeds up to 12 knots and carries
a crew of 86. The catamaran has a 142 ft. (115 ton)
cantilever mast which is raised from the deck for a
drilling operation.

activity: Men lowering a large stone from seasoning piles in an underground limestone mine.

te.text:
MINING STONE ON WILTSHIRE BORDER.      CH/BU

The OOLITIC Limestone or Bath stone quarries at Corsham and Box
on the Wiltshire border near Bath are unique in that the stone
is quarried from a mine 100 feet underground. The tunnels extend
for miles beneath the hillside and in one instance the shaft
enters the ground at one side of the hill and comes out three
miles away.  The stone is cut by means of huge saws and lifted
out by cranes and many of the stones weigh 12 tons. All stone
quarried in winter is left in mine until warmer days. Temper-
ature in mine is about 56 degrees all year round.

Photo shows- Like the ruins of some ancient city- Men lowering
a large stone from one of the immense piles which have been
standing for seasoning.
FOX March 2nd. 33.

activity: Three members of a housing association building bungalows on an estate.

te.text:
KENT PIONEERS BUILD THEIR OWN HOMES. MJH/RS.

On a housing estate in Hawes Lane Beckenham (Kent) men can
be seen working by floodlights on bungalows in various stages
of completion, sometimes up till ten o'clock at night. The
reason for this keen enthusiasm is that the men are working on their
own homes, or homes for their friends. Calling themselves, the
Beckenham Housing Association, this band of 25 pioneers includes
men from many trades - only a few are builders, the rest are
clerks, shopkeepers, cahiers, a post office engineer, etc, etc.,
but they are fast learning the art of house building as they work
with a will to erect their own homes. Order of priority is worked
out by friendly agreement and as each man works on a home for
his friend, he looks forward to the day when work will begin on
his own home.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: Three members of the Beckenham Housing
Association seen working on one of the bungalows on the Hawes Lane
estate. They are (left to right) COLIN MCDONALD; FRED
MATTINGLY: and LESLIE COOK. The men work on the estate in the
evenings when they have finished their own day's work, and at
weekends.
FOX PHOTOS MARCH 3RD. 1955. 515053.

FOX PHOTOS LTD.

LONDON, E.C.1.

te.text:
10 PER CENT OF WORKING TIME LOST ON FORD'S FACTORY.

It seems that Ford chief Sir Patrick Hennessy's accusation against the Trades Unions that up until October 30th, 81,000 working days were lost on the £30 million factory at Halewood, near Liverpool, because of labour disputes. The Company has just issued a statement in reply to Union protests against Sit Patrick's allegations disclosing that in fact, out of a possible 810,972 working days, 51,016 were lost because of weather, and a further 84,226 because of disputes. activity: Ex-miners manufacturing miniature pedal cars in a Pengam factory.

te.text:
KEN LAUDER          D.H.          15.2.56
MINERS MAKE MOTOR CARS.
Miners from the Welsh collieries are making
motor cars at Pengam (Monmouthshire), twelve
miles north of Cardiff.  But the motor cars
which they turn out from their clean, modern
factory are the kind that bring a sparkle into
the eyes of children.  For the factory was
started by the Austin Motor Company to employ
men who had left the mines, disabled by "dust
disease".  The miners, now 200 of them, have
taken so well to making the miniature pedal cars,
that they have produced 17,000 since the factory
was opened.  Thousands of these have been exported
to the U.S.A, Africa, Argentine, Canada and
Palestine.  Conditions of work at the factory are
supervised by a doctor.
O.P.S. 3-years-old Christopher Evans, a strictly
unofficial test driver, is watched by some of the
ex-miners who make the cars, which are the
production of their 'big brother' Austins. L. to
R. Alf Kent, 53 (from Grosfaen Colliery), Herbert
Price, 41, (from Markhal Colliery), Elwyn
Stephens, 43, (Bargoed Colliery) and Sydney Hoskins,
50 (Pengam).

FILE- INDUS. - FUEL + POWER - COAL
MINERS - WELFARE

te.text: Industry - Fuel and Power - Electricity - Power Stns - BANKSIDE.

244482   SKI
BANKSIDE POWER STATION: PRODUCTION GETS UNDER WAY
London: An industrial project which has aroused
much controversy from the time of its conception
has just gone into operation.
It is the Bankside Power Station, at which
the first 60,000-kilowatt turbo-alternator of about
80,000 horse-power, has started to supply electricity.
The project was allowed on condition that oil and not
coal was to be burned. Other conditions which had to
be observed were that the building must be set back
far enough from the Thames so as not to interfere with
the projected road and promenade.
Opposition to the Power station was so strong that
in January, 1947, a public inquiry was held, with the
result that the scheme was given Government sanction.
On completion the Bankside Power Station will
comprise four 60,000-kilowatt generating sets, the
oil consumption at full load (16-hour day) being
67 tons an hour, consuming in one winter's day about
850 tons.
PHOTO SHOWS: The control panel for boiler No.2 at
the Bankside Power Station.

activity: lifting an acetylene fractionating column at a chemical plant

te.text:
THE ONE THAT DIDN'T GET AWAY

A rather special acetylene fractionating column
is lifted into position at British Oxygen Chemicals'
plant at Maydown, Northern Ireland.

A month ago the column was in the news when it
broke in two while being towed across the Irish Sea
and half was partially submerged. It was salvaged
however and was erected on schedule.

The 42 ton, 137 ft. long column is part of a
£3 million acetylene plant being built by Fluor
(England) Ltd. for British Oxygen Chemicals.

NO REPRODUCTION FEE

Issued with the compliments of:
The British Oxygen Company Ltd.,
Hammersmith House, London, W.6.
RIVerside 2020
Mr. G.H. Metcalfe

te.text: FILE - PIGS - DH ONLY. INDUS - AGRIC.
FOR CONTACTS. SEE CHILDREN WITH ANIMALS.

GREAVES   D.H.   20.12.55.
A LITTLE PIG GOES TO MARKET.
The boys at the Church of England Home at Ashdon,
near Saffron Walden, Essex had a baby pig given to
them. They built a sty and have looked after it for
the past five months. They named it Biology and made
a real pet of it, but it has now grown into a fine
porker of 8 and a half score pounds. Today they got
up at 6-30am. washed and powdered Biology and took
her to Saffron Walden market. It was auctioned and
and brought the boys fourteen guineas, they now hope
to extend their piggy activities.
O.P.S. Some of the boys say good bye to Biology
at the pig sales.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY
21 DEC 1955

BIOLOGY the pig woke
early yesterday. She
had to be washed, pow-
dered and combed. For it
was market day at Saffron
Walden,
Biology, you see, is a fine
13-stone porker raised by
the 20 boys at the Church
of England home at Ash-
don, Essex. She was given
to them five months ago.
Ever since, they have been
fattennig her for the
Christmas market.
The boys turned up in
their school lunch break to
see Biology auctioned. And
before the bidding began,
they gave her a final
fattening sweet.
She fetched 14 guineas.

LONDON'S BIGGEST SPEED BOAT NEARS COMPLETION.

One of the world's largest motor-boats and the biggest ever built
in a London dockyard is nearing completion at Ferry Wharf, Isleworth.
The speed boat is 105-foot long and fitted with four 1,700
horse-power Bristol aircraft engines. With a cruising speed of
38 knots, she will be capable of making an Atlantic crossing
in three days.
Equipment includes hot and cold water supply, an electric cooker
and a refrigerator.
This craft was originally ordered two years ago together with

Atlantic. Only this one is being completed, work on the others

te.text:
2 7/8 wide x 2 5/8 deep

AND REVERSE

ROGER McPHEE talks to hens. He
talks to them about the weather
and politics and sport: he was say-
ing yesterday that his four Rhode
Island Reds, June, Henrietta, Mary
and Flossie, have become inter-
ested in football. Mr. McPhee,
aged 24, a pet shop manager, of
Hills Road, Cambridge, has noted
that eggs produced by his hens
tend to have double yolks. The
reason may, of course, be that he
has put the hens on a special diet.
But Mr. McPhee prefers to think
that is not the real reason. A man
likes to believe he can talk a
woman into anything.

SUN TONY EYLES 16-6-69
SHAGGY HEN STORY
Roger McPhee (24) of Cambridge seen talking to Henrietta, a 12 month old
Rhode Island Red. Mr. McPhee is always talking to his four hens - June
Henrietta, Mary and Flossie - he discusses the weather and politics and
feed them on a diet of crushed oats, flaked maize, rabbit pellets and racing
pigeon feed, in return the hens usually lay double yolked egges.

SUN
PROPERTY
17 JUN 1969
Please return

te.text:
£9,000  GOLD SERVICE OFF TO NORTH AMERICA    DG/own
BRITISH MASTERPIECE OF MODERN CRAFTSMANSHIP

Flying to North America  under armed escort
on Thursday (August 17th) is one of the most
valuable consignments of gold  ever to leave this
country.  While the amount  involved (400 ounces)
is not unprecedented,  the form it is taking - that
of an 18 carat  gold seven piece TEA AND COFFEE
SERVICE  considered to be  a masterpiece of
modern craftsmanship
The service which is insured  for £9,000  will  have
an armed police escort   from the BIRMINGHAM CITY
POLICE  on its journey from the workshops of  the
makers (Adie Brothers Birmingham  ) to  London
Airport.   Heaviest  piece of the service is the tray
- weighing  220 ounces - probably the largest  piece of
18ct gold assayed at the Birmingham Assay  Office
since its  opening.

PHOTO SHOWS:   Close up of the exquisite  chasing
on the  tea pot of the  £9000   GOLD SERVICE
which going on tour  of 25 cities in Canada
and the U. S. A.   Arthur Hudson  spent 350
hours chasing the work  has been a "chaser" for
48 years.
